maintopic: P.E.I. CAR FERRY SERVICE WOOD ISLAND-CARIBOU-NEW VESSEL
speechtext:
I should like to make an announcement pertaining to the automobile ferry service between Wood island, Prince Edward Island, and Caribou, Nova Scotia. At the present time the service is operated by the Northumberland Ferries Limited, which receives an annual subsidy of $158,000. The operation of this service is most important to the economy of Prince Edward Island, and the use made thereof in recent years has been increasing continuously.
While the economy of Prince Edward Island is well looked after by the Borden-Tormentine service in so far as railway communications are concerned and for highway traffic originating or terminating in the western section of the island, it has become increasingly important for the agricultural products of Prince Edward Island to be provided with an efficient automobile ferry service from the eastern part of the island to Nova Scotia. The present operator of this service finds it impossible to raise the necessary capital to acquire a new and more efficient vessel, in order to cope with the traffic offered.
I am pleased to announce to the house that the government has decided to construct a new automobile ferry vessel, which should be ready for operation in 1955. A decision has not yet been reached as to which agency will operate the service when the new vessel is ready to go into operation.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) of which I have given him notice. Can he enlighten the house on the implications of recent signs of growing anti-semitism in the Soviet union and the satellite countries in eastern Europe?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: ANTI-SEMITISM INQUIRY AS TO RECENT SIGNS OF GROWTH IN EASTERN EUROPE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. gentleman has said, he was good enough to give me notice of this important question.
The ominous and familiar pattern which seems to be developing within the soviet world is a matter which must be viewed with deepest anxiety-especially, if I may say so, by citizens of Jewish faith in Canada and other countries. Communist action against Jews has been recently highlighted in the purge in Czechoslovakia. There have been indications that similar purges may be in the making in other satellite capitals. The news from Moscow that six Jewish doctors have been arrested in that city, charged with fantastic and obviously trumped-up crimes,
Inquiries of the Ministry fits into the same pattern. There has not yet been time for the Department of External Affairs to receive sufficient information on this latest development to make possible a balanced assessment of its probable implications. That it may prove to be a very serious matter indeed is, I think, obvious to all of us.
Terrible atrocities stemmed from unbridled anti-semitism in nazi Germany. It would be a great tragedy and crime if the rulers of communist Russia were now planning to revive this dark and evil force from the past and to make use of it for their own ends.

speechtext:
The hon. member was good enough to give notice of his question to the Minister of Finance, and the minister asked me to thank him for that. Before leaving, the minister prepared an answer to the question, and he asked me to read it if the hon. member put his question today. The answer reads as follows:
I announced that the government had authorized an issue of $100 million par value 25 years 32 per cent bonds. These bonds will be sold in instalments to Bank of Canada which will in turn make the new issue available to investment dealers and banks for distribution among interested investors.
The new bonds will be dated January 15, 1953, will mature January 15, 1978, and are callable at 100 per cent and accrued interest at any time on or after January 15, 1975 on sixty days' notice.
I referred to the changes in market levels which have occurred in recent years, particularly since the time prior to the invasion of Korea when the last issue of long-term marketable bonds was made. I stated that the government had decided not to undertake at this time a conventional type of offering of the new issue of 25 year bonds. Nevertheless it is felt very desirable that steps should be taken to establish values in the longterm area in order to facilitate in due course a conventional offering of long-term bonds at some later date. Accordingly the new issue has been created and will be distributed by sale in instalments to Bank of Canada and subsequent sales by Bank of Canada in the market from time to time at prevailing prices. The proceeds of the loan will be paid into the consolidated revenue fund and will be disbursed for general purposes of the government.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the seriousness of what the government has been caught doing is far worse now in view of what the Minister of National Defence said on Tuesday and in view of the correspondence with Mr. Currie that he placed upon Hansard. At the moment I refer to the correspondence that he intended to place on Hansard, not the letter that he placed there inadvertently. When one reads that correspondence and when one takes note of what the Minister of National Defence had to say the other day, it becomes clear that Mr. Currie did not want to submit his first draft to anyone in the department for the purpose of looking it over. I remind the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) that on December 17, when he made his statement on this matter and answered certain questions, he made a definite statement in answer to a question of mine. As reported at page 829 of Hansard, I asked whether it was the general practice, as to reports which are made on any particular department, to refer them to the head of that department before the report is presented. In part of his reply the Prime Minister said:
I was quite surprised to learn that this investigator had felt that it was the proper thing to he done.
I think all of us who were here in the house at the time remember the forthrightness with which the Prime Minister made that statement. I for one shared his surprise that anyone would think that this was the proper


thing to do. But, Mr. Speaker, as a result of what the Minister of National Defence said on Tuesday and as a result of his tabling his correspondence with Mr. Currie, it now comes out that Mr. Currie did not think it was the thing to be done. Mr. Currie was opposed to showing to the department an earlier copy of the report that he eventually made to the minister. Not only was he opposed in the first instance to showing a copy, but Mr. Drury, the deputy minister, agreed with Mr. Currie that that should not be done. But despite the reluctance or the disinclination of Mr. Currie to show an advance copy to the department, despite his contention that it should not be done, despite the agreement that Mr. Drury expressed with that position, the Minister of National Defence suggested to Mr. Drury that he press Mr. Currie on the point; and it was only after the Minister of National Defence got into the picture and put that pressure upon Mr. Currie that he finally, reluctantly and despite his disinclination to do so, let the department see the report on certain conditions which he spells out in his letter.
When I put my question to the Prime Minister on December 17, he said that he was surprised that Mr. Currie thought this was a proper thing to have done. If he was surprised that Mr. Currie thought it was a proper thing to be done, what does he think now? Does he not think that he owes an apology to Mr. Currie for suggesting that Mr. Currie thought this was a proper thing to be done, when it is clear that Mr. Currie had no such view? What does the Prime Minister think now of the Minister of National Defence who was responsible for this course of action at which the Prime Minister was surprised? Not only did the Prime Minister give the answer to my question which I have already read, but in his own prepared statement that he gave us that morning of December 17, 1952, as reported at page 827 of Hansard he said this:
The inquiries also disclosed that Mr, Currie and his representatives discussed this matter with the deputy minister and that the suggestion was made that the deputy minister might go over the draft, when it was ready, and point out any inaccuracies in the facts reported which had been obtained from the department itself. The deputy minister mentioned this suggestion to the minister and the minister authorized him to go over this draft but told him to be extremely careful to make no comment about anything but the facts that had been obtained from the department.
I admit that that statement is capable of different interpretations, if one wants to put different interpretations on it. But the plain and simple interpretation that seems to me to arise from it is that the Prime Minister, when he made his inquiries following my question on December 17, was informed that

the suggestion that the report should be seen in the department first emanated from Mr. Currie, that it went from Mr. Currie to Mr. Drury and then that Mr. Drury reported that to his minister, the Minister of National Defence, and that the Minister of National Defence agreed. But the story that the Minister of National Defence told us on Tuesday of this week puts it in reverse. From the minister's statement as well as from Mr. Currie's letter, it is clear that the idea of this report being "vetted" in the department did not originate with Mr. Currie. It originated in the department. When Mr. Currie refused, the minister himself took the opposite position, and he has to take the full responsibility for being the one to put pressure upon Mr. Currie to do what Mr. Currie did not want to do and (to do what the Prime Minister on December 17 said he was surprised to learn had been done. I therefore submit that this question is a fair one to ask the Prime Minister: Is it not time that he made an apology to Mr. Currie, and what is he going to do about the action of the Minister of National Defence in putting that improper pressure upon Mr. Currie?
Mr. Speaker, I understand why the government is trying to find some red herring, some way in which to becloud this issue; because the plain fact is that they are caught in the act right down the line. The Minister of National Defence stood up here in the house the other day and said that what he wanted, when he asked Mr. Currie to make this investigation, was the truth. Those were his words: "I wanted the truth". It now turns out that he wanted some official of his to see that truth before it was put in final form to be presented to parliament. What kind of truth is that that one is asking for if, when your department is being investigated, you ask for the right to have the so-called truth about your department "vetted" before it is put before parliament?
The Solicitor General (Mr. Campney) referred to this matter when he spoke on December 17 and suggested to us in this house that we should be extremely grateful to the Minister of National Defence for letting us have this report. After all, according to him, it was just a little personal document out of the minister's desire to have the truth about his department, and he was exceedingly generous-he was courageous-in letting us have it; and we should show our appreciation of that courage and of that generosity by not making such open attacks on the Minister of National Defence.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the more one goes into this whole story the more it is true to say in this very simple language,
Committee on Defence Expenditure the government has been caught in the act of doing things that it had no right to do as the government of a democratic country. I suggest that someone has got to clear up this discrepancy in the reports given to us on December 17 by the Prime Minister, and on Tuesday of this week by the Minister of National Defence, and that in that connection we have got to know just where the cabinet stands on this whole issue of how this question was handled.
Now, Mr. Speaker, not only has the government been caught in the act of making these changes and of pressing Mr. Currie to do something that he did not want to do, but the government has, as I said on Tuesday night, been caught permitting its top military people to take unto themselves authority and a position which it is not correct for them to take in a democratic state. I want to come back to that for just a minute, Mr. Speaker, because I felt on Tuesday night that that was the most important-
Time.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: -part of what I had to say at that time, namely, that the most serious issue-
Time.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext: Order. The hon. member's time has expired, and he may continue only with the unanimous consent of the house.
Go ahead.
No.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext: Is it agreed?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I thank the house, Mr. Speaker. I shall be just a very few minutes.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Go ahead.
You can't take it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext: Order. I gathered that there was general consent to the hon. member continuing.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I sincerely thank you, Mr. Speaker, and the house. I shall express that appreciation by being just as brief as I can.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
And I thank the house for their approval of that sentiment, too. Therefore for a minute or two we are on good terms. But I now want to repeat and underline the importance of the issue which I raised on Tuesday night, namely, that we are in a very bad way in a democracy if we allow the military people, the top brass, to assume an attitude of superiority to the civil authority, to the elected government
1018	HOUSE OF
Committee on Defence Expenditure of this country. I need not repeat at this time the five examples that I gave on Tuesday night of ways in which, in my view, the military people, the chief of the general staff, and the officials of the minister's department, have been dictating to the government, yes, dictating to the Prime Minister, in a way that they have no right to do, and I call upon this government to put the military in the place in which it belongs as the servant of the state.
Now, with this I will close. I just wish to give the house three or four quotations from the debate-
Give us your amendment.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I have already given the amendment to the Speaker, and I shall put it when I sit down. I have already indicated to the house that in my view the Sandys case of 1938-in the United Kingdom parliament-is one that this government should study very closely. Here was a case where, when the attorney general of that government interrogated a member of parliament as to where he got certain information, it became not a question that was referred to the police, not a question for further threats, but a question for an important historical constitutional procedural debate in the mother of parliaments that took place on June 29, 1938. It covers eighty columns or forty pages of the British Hansard, so obviously I cannot read very much of it. But let me give one or two quotations from some of the really important people who took part in that debate. For example, at column 2166 I find the Right Hon. Clement Attlee said this:
If it is once thought that members of this house can be brought up and interrogated and obliged to give up the sources of their information when they speak in this house, on the ground that it was suspected they were using official information improperly got, there would soon come a cutting away of members of this house from the public service, and there would be apprehension among members of the public service when mixing with members of parliament. They might easily say something which a member might use afterwards, and it might be traced to them.
That is part of a lengthy speech in which Mr. Attlee emphasizes the importance of the principle that was at stake, the right of individual members of parliament to receive information and to use that information in whatever way they thought was best for the good of the state without being pilloried by the executive of the day.
Similarly, the Right Hon. Winston Churchill spoke in the same debate, and it is a Chur-chillian masterpiece which I shall not attempt to read in full, in which he said in part:
A member of parliament has a duty to discharge. If he has information he must try his best to make


that information effective upon the government. He must make sure that a minister knows the truth.
He goes on to say that even if it is unpalatable truth he must get it to the minister, even if he has to use it in debate or in question time in the house.
He goes on to tell of his own experience at times when information came into his possession, perhaps a little irregularly, but information which he was able to use to the advantage of the state. While telling of one of these experiences he said:
But I am bound to say that it came to me with a shock of astonishment to learn that he would have been entitled to send the attorney general to me to ask me where I got that information.
Mr. Churchill was referring to the prime minister. His speech is to be found from column 2173 to column 2182 in the British Hansard of June 30, 1938. Later on in the speech he gives five or six examples, some of them involving himself, some of them involving others, where information leaked out which members of parliament were able to bring to the attention of the government, with the result that real good was done to the state.
Then I turn to Sir Archibald Sinclair. Let us bring a Liberal into this as well, and I find that at column 2171 he said:
Certainly, the government have the right to exact strict loyalty, discretion and obedience from their servants, but members of parliament are responsible to the people whom they represent in this house. They are not responsible to the attorney-general or to any minister of the government. It would be deplorable if all sources of information were dried up. There may be some dangers, but there are great safeguards. There is the power of Mr. Speaker to disallow questions. There are great safeguards, and there are still graver dangers in the encroachment of the executive upon the rights of parliament.
That is something that this government should pay some attention to, and they should note the next sentence which fits so well here:
Governments are too apt to confuse danger to themselves with danger to the state.
Then my last quotation, Mr. Speaker, comes from Mr. Arthur Henderson and is found at column 2194 of the same Hansard in which he said in concluding a very effective speech:
Once you destroy parliamentary privilege and make it impossible for members of parliament to listen to anyone who comes to them with information which, rightly or wrongly, is conceived to be in the public interest and which that member of parliament should receive, issues will be raised which will strike at the very foundations of parliament. I hope that it will now be decided beyond a peradventure that the privileges of this house are still to be maintained and will be enforced, in order to protect any hon. member in relation to his parliamentary duties.
It is unnecessary for me to comment, Mr. Speaker. These quotations speak for themselves, and I feel I should respect the

privilege the house has given me to go on for these extra minutes by taking no more time on this occasion. Therefore I will conclude at this time by moving, seconded by my deskmate, the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright):
That the amendment be amended by adding thereto the following words:
"and to give consideration to the desirability of recommending that Mr. Currie be asked to conduct a further inquiry into any other expenditures and commitments covered by the terms of this resolution."

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext:
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre mentioned his amendment the other evening, and I have had an opportunity of considering it. It gives me some concern, in several aspects. I think the house has agreed that consideration can be given to directing a committee to do something which it has the power to do, but which it might otherwise not do. This amendment would come within that ruling.
However, there is a limit to what a committee can do. A committee obviously can do what is included in the terms of a motion under which the committee is set up. There are also other incidental things that the committee can do.
Would the recommendation to retain Mr. Currie to continue his inquiry be a recommendation which that committee could make to the house? The committee obviously could not direct Mr. Currie to do that, by itself. The recommendation, if made by the committee, would be to continue an inquiry that Mr. Currie had started, and the report of which is before the committee.
After giving that point careful consideration-and I do not think I shall hear argument on it-I have come to the conclusion that on that ground the amendment should be allowed to stand. But I should point out the reason I am allowing it to stand on that ground is that it would be a recommendation that the person who made the report should continue.
There is also a technical point which I could raise, and that is whether the amendment is an amendment to the amendment or an amendment to the main motion. I think if I were being very technical

for which I hope I have not a reputation-I could consider that as a serious argument.
In allowing the amendment to stand I do not want it to be considered a precedent which must be followed.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. Si. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope no one will have the impression that because I rise at this moment I intend to question the ruling you have just made. Nothing would be farther from my thoughts than to do that.
Committee on Defence Expenditure
I would not have considered it necessary, or even useful, to enter again into this debate on the Currie report, were it not for two speeches made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), and particularly for the one he has just concluded. But I feel very strongly about two aspects of those speeches, not so much because of their bearing on the present situation, but because of their possible effect on the thinking in this House of Commons, and among the public, about proper democratic processes, and the proper relationship between the civilian authority and the armed forces on the one hand, and the proper conduct of the executive and of members of parliament in relation to public affairs-and even in relation to party strife between groups of members of parliament in relation to public affairs.
Now, the hon. gentleman is sometimes inclined to set himself up not only as an authority, having made profound studies of parliamentary practices, constitutional traditions and parliamentary rules of procedure, but also as an example of rectitude for the rest of us to follow in our own public conduct. There seems to have been some indication at least on this occasion that members of the official opposition, by their applause, are taking the hon. gentleman at his own valuation.
Because of that I feel that, having a responsibility of leadership in this house, I would be remiss in my duty if, by my silence, I allowed the impression to be created that I agreed with any of the views expressed by the hon. gentleman on those two main branches, namely the proper relationship between the civilian authority and those responsible for the armed forces, and the proper relationship between the executive and members of parliament, and between members of parliament and the general public, and the manner in which it is proper for them to envisage their responsibility, and to shape their conduct accordingly.
Now, I wish to make it quite clear that I cannot agree with the hon. member on those aspects. I wish first of all to deal with the proper relationship between the civilian authority and those responsible for the organization and the training and-yes-the fighting of our armed forces, when they have to fight.
There is no doubt that under our system it is the civilian authority that is supreme; but there is also no doubt that those at the head of our armies do, as they have done ever since we have had armed forces, carry and discharge very heavy responsibilities to the nation to which they belong.

We all agree with that.

Committee on Defence Expenditure

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Now, the hon. gentleman seems to suggest that, whatever happens or whatever is said about them, they must remain silent, and still be satisfied to carry on and to discharge their heavy responsibilities.
Well, with that I do not agree. Nor do I agree with the suggestion of the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) that they have to be dumb, so far as everybody else is concerned, and not utter a word, except through the minister.
Mr. Speaker-
Sit down.
The Prime Minister has said that I suggested they should be dumb. I did not suggest they should be dumb. I said they should speak through the minister who represents them.
The same thing.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I wish first of all to call attention to some of the expressions used by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre on Tuesday. At page 968 of Hansard he is reported to have said this:
The point that we feel is most serious about this whole business is the question as to the proper place of the armed forces in a democracy. Are they the servant of the state, of the people of the country through their elected representatives, or are they in charge? Are the armed forces entitled to dictate to the government and to push other people around? In our view there has been too much evidence of that attitude throughout this whole business, and that is our primary concern at the present time.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I have not had any evidence of dictation to the government or of pushing people around. The hon. gentleman went on to say:
Hon. members will recall that, when he-
The Prime Minister.
-tabled the report, he placed on Hansard at the same time a memorandum from the chief of the general staff. During the course of his remarks at that time he stated that he was giving us that memorandum because the chief of the general staff thought that the views contained in that memorandum should be given publicity at the same time as the revelations contained in the Currie report itself. When the Prime Minister was questioned by my deskmate, the hon. member for Melfort, during the course of debate in the next day or so as to why he had done this, the Prime Minister interjected to say that he was prepared to give the answer right then and there. He said he did it because he was requested to do so by the chief of the general staff. In our view, Mr. Speaker, the chief of the general staff had no right to ask the elected Prime Minister of this country to table that memorandum, and in our view the Prime Minister had no right to accede to that request.
I take full responsibility, Mr. Speaker, for having acceded to that request and I disagree with the hon. gentleman in his statement
[Mr. Harkness.l

that the chief of the general staff had no right to make that request. I submit that he had a perfect right to make that request and that it was a request about which I had to take the responsibility. I did take the responsibility of putting that document before the house at the same time I tabled the report, and I did so because there was a certain part of that report which, though it was a report dealing with only the works branch of the army, might be interpreted as applying to the whole army. If it were interpreted in that way it was in my opinion, as in the opinion of the general staff stated to me, something that would be very damaging to the organization and morale of our army.
What is it that is contained in the memorandum? It is printed at page 640 of Hansard and reads as follows:
Army Headquarters Ottawa, 15 December, 1952
The Minister
I have read the report on the investigation of army works services by Mr. George Currie.
He reaches conclusions and makes recommendations which must be the subject of careful study before I am in a position to advise you as to the extent to which remedial action has already been taken and what other steps I would recommend.
In defining his task Mr. Currie states "I have conducted an investigation into the deficiencies and other irregularities of the engineering detachment of the army works services at Petawawa and elsewhere".
However, included in Mr. Currie's report are statements which may be interpreted by the public as a condemnation of the competence, integrity and efficiency of the army as a whole. I refer particularly to the statements in the last paragraph of part 1 of his report.
This has already been referred to in the house as page 17 of the offset reproduction of the report. I continue:
I understand this report is to be made public and if such statements made by Mr. Currie are interpreted by the public and the serviceman as having reference to the army as a whole the effect will be most damaging.
I, therefore, request that Mr. Currie clarify publicly whether such statements are intended to refer, as his quoted opening remarks would appear to indicate, to the engineering work services only, or whether they are intended to refer to the Canadian army as a whole. If the latter is the intention then I would further request that Mr. Currie provide publicly the facts upon which such opinions and observations are based.
Under the National Defence Act the chief of the general staff has the responsibility for the Canadian army, and if a statement is made and put forward by the government without any qualification, or any hint that it does not agree with it, that is interpreted as reflecting upon the competence, integrity and efficiency of the army as a whole, I think it is the duty of the chief of the general staff to wish to have that cleared up, and if that is the conclusion that is ultimately arrived

at I am sure that anyone worthy of becoming at any time the chief of the general staff would feel that he could do nothing but abandon his position and let somebody else take over the responsibility who is going to discharge it in a more competent and efficient manner.
Here in this country, you know, public service, not only on the civilian side but on the military side as well, is provided by men many of whom do so at personal sacrifice of their own pecuniary interests, and the main and practically the only compensation they get for the sacrifice they make is the personal satisfaction of feeling that they are doing something useful for their nation and their fellow citizens. When it becomes apparent that they can no longer have that feeling, or can have the feeling that it is shared by those with whom they are performing that work, then there is no further reason for them to continue in office. Does anyone imagine, Mr. Speaker, that I would be doing for anyone but the public service what I have been doing for the last four or five years for the pecuniary compensation that I get for it?
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Does anyone imagine that the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) did what he did during the war years for the pecuniary compensation he got out of it? Fortunately there are many in this country- and I think it would include practically everybody in this house-who feel that when there is a service to be performed for the country and for their fellow citizens it is not the pecuniary compensation that is going to entice them to give that service. It is for the moral satisfaction they get out of it that they are doing their part, as their ancestors before them did their part, to build up the country and to pass it on to future generations as a good country of which to be a citizen and a good country in which to live.
All that was requested by the chief of the general staff was that if this document, which might have that ambiguous implication, were going to be made public, there should be an opportunity for clearing up the ambiguity and saying whether or not it did refer to the competence and integrity of the whole army set-up or whether it referred to the few crooks-and I am paraphrasing the expression used in the report-who had been guilty of irregularities, yes of crimes, for which our courts of justice have meted out to them the sentences they are now serving in our penal institutions.
If, in attempting to clear up that ambiguity, it was cleared up in a way that might reflect upon the competence and integrity of the
Committee on Defence Expenditure whole army, then the chief of the general staff requested that further facts be made public to show on what the condemnation of their competence and efficiency was based. I think that it was not only the right but the responsibility and duty of the chief of the general staff to all the loyal officers and men under his command to take that position and to ask that the ambiguity be cleared up, and if it were maintained that a reflection was meant to be cast upon the efficiency of the whole service, then the facts upon which that assertion was made should be made public so that effective methods could be adopted to have and to maintain in this country the kind of competent and honest military forces upon which we have fortunately had the privilege of relying in two world wars where perhaps our very existence as a nation was at stake.
A second point with which I wish to deal is the statement made by the hon. gentleman that the chief of staff had no right to say- and I think his words were-"to the personnel of the service and the employees of national defence" that they were not to discuss the Currie report. Again, the hon. gentleman knows that the chief of staff never attempted to make such a suggestion to the employees of the Department of National Defence. The hon. gentleman knows that that direction was given on December 15 in the form of a signal which reads as follows:
From: Can Army
To: Wescom, Pracom, Cencom, Quecom, Eascom
For GOC from CGS.
Now, I take it that means: From Canadian army headquarters to western command, prairie command, central command, Quebec command, and eastern command, for general officer commanding from chief of general staff.
Para One The report covering the investigation by Mr. George Currie of the army works services is about to be tabled in the House of Commons.
Para Two It is possible that interested parties may attempt to obtain comments on this report from serving personnel. I would therefore remind you that this report is a privileged document in the hands of the government and it is obviously improper at this time for any serving officer or man to make any comment on it.
"Privileged document" I take it here is not "privileged document" as my hon. friend from Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) and I, in court parlance, would understand it. We would probably not describe that as a privileged document although it was a document which was in the hands of the government and which was about to be tabled in the
1022	HOUSE OF
Committee on Defence Expenditure House of Commons. I think that this was a wise direction to say that possibly-
-interested parties may attempt to obtain comments on this report from serving personnel.
And-
-it is obviously improper at this time for any serving officer or man to make any comment on it.
Now, that is the second incident of the "dictation" referred to by my hon. friend, and to the "pushing around" referred to by him.
Are they free to discuss it now?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not think it would be proper for them to be discussing it. I think that it is proper for them to wait until there has been some opportunity to obtain that clarification of the ambiguous portion to which the chief of staff refers in the memorandum addressed to his minister and with which, because of the absence of his minister, he asked me to deal.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Would the Prime Minister permit a question? Does the Prime Minister know whether there was any order by the chief of the general staff requesting "that no discussion be entered into by employees of the Department of National Defence on the m/n report"-the reference being to the Currie report? If the Prime Minister does not know of any such order, perhaps I can have this little slip investigated.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think the hon. gentleman had better have that little slip investigated because the information I received was that the only direction given by the chief of staff was the direction that is- included in this signal which went out from headquarters on December 15. That is the information I have and I have information that implies that there was no other attempted instruction given by the chief of staff.
In connection with that matter what the hon. gentleman said was:
Indeed as I have said, I read with interest in the press that the chief of the general staff had issued orders that members of the armed forces and employees of national defence were requested not to discuss the Currie report.
I have seen nothing in the press to that effect and the information I received is that this signal to the general officers commanding the various military commands throughout the country was the only direction given.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: When the Prime Minister is through I will come across and show him the slip to which I refer.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has already shown me something the source of


which has become a matter of considerable concern not only to me but to a great many of the public.
A red herring.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am not anxious to share any confidences with the hon. gentleman which have been obtained in the way in which it appears that a copy of Mr. Currie's work was obtained.
The hon. gentleman went on to say that- -while the chief of the general staff denies to the people to whom he can issue orders the right to discuss the Currie report, he does not hesitate to discuss it himself.
I assume that the hon. gentleman was referring to the terms of the memorandum I have just read. I submit that that memorandum is no discussion of the Currie report. It is a request that what the chief of staff looked upon as an ambiguity, an unfortunate ambiguity in the report, might be cleared up.
Another point with which I would like to deal quite briefly is the Canadian Army Journal to which the hon. gentleman referred. Now, I have here a copy of the Canadian Army Journal, the December number, and I have been informed that the message to the Canadian army from the chief of the general staff was written and sent in for inclusion in that publication in November before any part of the working papers or of the Currie report had come before the Department of National Defence-and long before there had been any criticism in this house of anything referred to in the Currie report. Now, the hon. gentleman has been very severe in the language he used with respect to this general message from the chief of staff to the Canadian army. It is true that the effect of this message was featured quite prominently in Canadian press dispatches that were published, perhaps before the first one I saw which was in a newspaper dated January 13. But it is not surprising that the press should, even if it had this for weeks, think that it was something of interest to the reading public to be featured in its news columns at that time.
This message was written because of a large number of critical references to incidents occurring in the army, and published over a period of months in some of the Canadian newspapers. The copy of his message to the Canadian army written by the chief of staff has annexed to it a large number of newspaper clippings, none of them subsequent to the date of the first showing of the working paper for the Currie report to the deputy minister of national defence. Now, I think that this message from the chief of the general staff to the Canadian army is quite a proper message for one to

issue to personnel for whose morale he is responsible, as he is for the competence and efficiency of the army of which he is the chief. That is all I wish to say about these relations between the civilian authority and the army. No one will gainsay that under our system the civilian authority is supreme in our constitutional set-up, but no one will gainsay that the armed forces are essential to the subsistence of our constitutional setup, and no one will gainsay that their competence and efficiency depends to a certain degree upon the respect in which those who are at the head are held, and are entitled to be held, by the nation which they serve.
Now, the second matter with which I shall deal is the receipt and use of a stolen working paper, prepared on behalf of a professional man, and which the hon. gentleman thought it was his duty, in the public interest, to use in this house.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: On a point of privilege, Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) if he is in a position to say categorically that it was a stolen copy?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think I will be in a, position, within a very short time, not only to say that it is a stolen document but to say who stole it. But just drawing conclusions from obvious facts, I think it is quite obvious that that document was not obtained from the Department of National Defence. There was only one copy delivered to the Department of National Defence on November 27, and it was returned to Mr. Currie's partner on December 8 when the signed report was then delivered to the department.
The information contained in Mr. Currie's letter is to the effect that there were only ten copies of the offset pages stitched together, and his investigation had been such that he was able to account for all ten of them. There had been additional pages, some ninety or more perhaps, which had been prepared at the same time in the printer's office and neither Mr. Currie nor the printer was able to account for every copy of every page that had been offset in the same process and at the same time. At first he did not believe the copy was one of the offset copies, but it turned out to be one of them. He was allowed by the hon. gentleman to inspect the copy, and he and his representatives satisfied themselves that it was one of the same offset copies as had been prepared by this printing firm.
Now, that copy found its way into the hands of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). At that time it did not appear to be very serious. This was a
15, 1953	1023
Committee on Defence Expenditure document that was going to be tabled, and whether or not one got advance information about it did not seem to be very important. When the hon. gentleman first mentioned it here on December 15 he was quite surprised that there had been, in the report as finalized and signed, any modification from the working paper of which he had a copy. But when he spoke on December 17, and when he spoke yesterday and again today, he knew from the information that I had given to the house that this was not a report nor a copy of the report, but this was a preliminary working paper which had not been completed, which had not been signed and which differed in some respects from the report which was made and which was signed.
There is no other possible suggestion for it being elsewhere than in the printer's office than the suggestion that someone improperly took it out of the printer's office and delivered it to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar.
It might have blown out of the window.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, those pages had not been stitched together, and I do not think the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) would seriously suggest that it would so happen that 74 pages would be blown out a window, picked up in the alley and from there brought to the member for Rosetown-Biggar.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That would be an ill wind that blew the Liberals no good.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The experience of the Liberals has not been that Providence treats them in that unkind way.
Now, I am assuming that this copy was taken without Mr. Currie's consent or without the consent of anyone authorized to give consent on Mr. Currie's behalf, and without the printer's consent or the consent of anyone authorized to give consent on the printer's behalf. In common parlance that is usually referred to as stealing. The whole situation has all the earmarks of the copy having been taken away in a manner which is called theft. I would think that possibly under the circumstances there would be such public-spirited citizens that, if they felt they had come in any way into possession of information that was essentially of interest to the security of the state, and that they did not trust the members of the government or any supporter of the government with that information, they might think it was a proper thing to convey it to somebody other than a member of the government or a supporter of the government. But I think that the obvious choice they would make would be

Committee on Defence Expenditure to convey it to the leader of the official opposition whose duty it is to see to it that information of real interest to the public becomes available to the public. This document did not go to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew). It went to my hon. friend's leader who has not yet become the leader of the official opposition.
And never will.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not want to make any prophecies. After all, I am in my own country, and no one is a good prophet in his own country. I therefore leave it to the hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser). However that may be, the fact that this document did not go to the leader of the official opposition seems to nullify the suggestion that it might be in the discharge of a patriotic urge to save the country that it was being communicated. I am not saying that this was the case, but if it was being handed to the leader of the C.C.F. group as an implement to be used in party strife, all I can say is that I would deprecate it greatly if our politics sank to the level where, in the conduct of our strife with each other, we had to have agents to steal confidential documents or had to have agents to tap telephone wires.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is something of the same nature and something about which-
The government of which you were a member was the one to have that done.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sorry but I did not catch that interjection. This amplification system is convenient in some ways but it does not allow you to catch all the interjections which come from the various corners of the house.
Especially those you do not want to hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I will tell my hon. friend that, except when he is making a long and repetitious speech, I like to hear what he has to say.
The same thing may be said about others.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think there are privileges that members of parliament have, and that those privileges are not only sacred to them but are essential to the proper functioning of our democratic institutions. Quite frankly, however, I may say that I do not think those privileges require us to receive stolen property and to make use of it. We are all of us responsible to the public and each one of us is responsible to the electors of his constituency. I do not think that anyone wants

to set himself up as too severe a judge of others; but there are definitely implications-
Mr. Speaker, I have no brief for anyone but I do not think that the Prime Minister-
Sit down.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. I do not think that the Prime Minister or anyone else in this house has a right to say of a member of parliament that he is a receiver of stolen goods.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not want to insist upon a technical legal definition.
I should hope not.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: But I suggest that no one is entitled, because of his privileges as a member of parliament, to have in his possession a thing that has been stolen if he knows it was stolen.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of privilege. Is the Prime Minister suggesting that my leader knew that he was receiving a stolen document?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am not making any suggestion at all. I am merely commenting upon facts which are already notorious to the Canadian public.

Mr. Speaker, I rise again on a question of privilege. I think that, on mature reflection, the Prime Minister will realize that statements like that should not be made. The other day, Mr. Speaker, you ruled that a suggestion about independence-
Order.

Oh yes, Mr. Speaker, you ruled that even a suggestion from this side of the house that members were not independent was dangerous to the privileges of parliament. I hold no brief for wrongdoing, and I know nothing about this matter; but surely the Prime Minister dare not make such statements.
I am subject to your direction, Mr. Speaker.

I rise on a question of privilege. In my opinion-and I think a reading of Hansard will prove that I am right-the Prime Minister has implied that the leader of this group received stolen property knowing that it was stolen.
No.
Yes.
I think a reading of Hansard will indicate that; and I would ask you, Mr. Speaker, to ask the Prime Minister to withdraw any such implication.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext: I did not understand the Prime Minister to make that statement. I will leave it to him. The Prime Minister knows whether or not he made that statement.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What I stated was that this was a stolen document, and that, prior to coming into the possession of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), it was in the hands of the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). I do not know how it got there, but it is a stolen document. To anyone who does not know any more than I know about it, it appears to be a stolen document. I think that anyone who has it would feel some concern as to whether or not it was a stolen document.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on this point of order or question of privilege, may I say that I feel it is a particularly serious matter, especially in view of the unfortunate absence of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. The Prime Minister keeps using language that suggests that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar knew, when he received this document, that it was stolen, and I object to that language.
No.
Yes.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Mr. Speaker,-

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext: Order. I cannot hear what is being said because there are so many interruptions.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: If the Prime Minister did not mean that and will say clearly that he did not mean it, I will not press the point further. May I remind you, Mr. Speaker, that, in addition to this language, a few minutes ago the Prime Minister said he did not think it was necessary for us in parliament, in the pursuit of our privileges, to have agents out getting this kind of property. That is a suggestion that my leader had an agent out trying to get this property, something which is completely false. As a matter of fact-

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext: Order. That point can be denied later on.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I deny it categorically.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext: The question I am concerned with at the moment is whether the Prime Minister has at this time stated that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar received the report knowing, at the time he received it, that it was stolen. I did not understand him to say so. I should like to clear up that point.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I did not intend to say that he knew it. I intended to suggest that circumstances were such that he might very
Committee on Defence Expenditure well be thought to have known it. I do not know whether he did or not-I hope he did not.
Why don't you clean the whole thing up by withdrawing?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am not going to clean the whole thing up by withdrawing anything I have said because I cannot, by anything I say, manufacture facts nor alter facts that have taken place.
Now, with respect to the suggestion that the letter printed in Hansard of Tuesday constitutes a threat, I cannot read it as being such. Was it, or was it not, proper that any efforts be made to find out how this confidential document went from the printer's office to somewhere else? I say from the printer's office, though until the matter is cleared up there could be suspicion on every person connected with both the printer's office and Mr. Currie's office.
It is known-and it is nothing to be ashamed of-that both in the printer's office and in Mr. Currie's office there are people who take an active interest in party politics, and who have done so, exercising their proper democratic right. Until this matter is cleared up everyone who could possibly have done this thing of communicating one of Mr. Currie's working papers to somebody unauthorized to have it is equally subject to suspicion. All that was said to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar was to notify him that at Mr. Currie's suggestion the R.C.M.P. were being-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Perhaps there was no suggestion about the R.C.M.P., but Mr. Currie's suggestion that there might be further investigation. The R.C.M.P. were being asked to make that further investigation. Well, what would the hon. gentleman have said about the Minister of National Defence if he had requested that the R.C.M.P. continue that investigation without giving any notice whatsoever to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar? This is merely information that the R.C.M.P. is being asked to follow up the investigation that Mr. Currie has been making, and the suggestion that if he felt it proper to say where the document came from it might facilitate the investigation. There is no veiled threat there, no attempt to coerce, no attempt to put pressure upon anybody, and no attempt to draw any red herrings across the situation that the hon. gentleman qualifies as "having been caught in the act". That is a suggestion made with respect to the
1026	HOUSE OF
Committee on Defence Expenditure changes that appeared between the working paper and the draft that was finally signed by Mr. Currie.
Those changes were made entirely upon the responsibility of Mr. Currie, who was making a report to the Minister of National Defence, not a report to the House of Commons, not a report to the governor in council, but to the head of the Department of National Defence. I was surprised that there had been any prior discussion of the terms in which that report was to be made. But the hon. gentleman and I do know that when the Mainguy report about the navy was published it did contain factual mistakes that were used in an effort to throw some discredit upon it. And I do not think it is strange that the minister should have hoped that this report would be as free from mistakes, factual mistakes, as possible.
The thing that I wonder at is that there were not more comments made to Mr. Currie's representatives about some other things which appear to be factual mistakes in the terms of this report. As I remember it, there was not anything at all said about the horses, and we now have it quite clear that there were no non-existent persons placed on the payroll, and there were no horses placed on the payroll. Perhaps I might take this opportunity of referring to a remark of the hon. member for Nanaimo in his interesting speech, following the Minister of National Defence, that because I had made a qualification about the information I got, we appeared to be more ready to accept the testimony of a man who is now in the penitentiary than the categorical affirmation of Mr. George Currie.
Well, I hope the hon. gentleman understood that when I was making that qualification it referred only to such matters as were not those that would appear in the official documents. The names of all those who were put on the payroll are on the payroll, and they are all names of existing persons. What I was qualifying-
They were playing proxies for the horses.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Well, perhaps the hon.
gentleman has not had the experience I have had of acting sometimes as a teamster. I do not think that the teamster is a proxy for the horses that are pulling the load. What I was making the qualification about was as to the refund that was handed back by the teamsters to Sergeant Young who had provided the horses. That does not appear on the payroll. That information was gathered from written confessions made by Sergeant Young both to the provost corps officials and to the R.C.M.P.


Now, he is a man who has been convicted and who is now in the penitentiary. Like the hon. member for Nanaimo, I would not care to vouch for the absolute accuracy of everything he said. His statement was that the teamsters retained the ordinary 75 cents plus 5 cents and refunded the remainder to him. Now, that cannot be checked from official records. That is an illegal, irregular transaction that took place between these teamsters and Sergeant Young, and that was the part of my statement upon which I was making the qualification.
While I am dealing with them, I should like to refer to one other point. On Tuesday night the Leader of the Opposition made a broadcast on the Canadian network, the text of which had gone out and was distributed for release at 7.45 eastern standard time. I have it on good authority, from persons who listened to the broadcast, that there were some additions in what went over the air that were not in the text. The reference in the text to the Petawawa horses is this:
The thought of horses on the payroll in the name of non-existent men has been a cause of merriment, and understandably.
It certainly has been the cause of merriment, and the subject of some pretty clever cartoons. I have it from the testimony of persons who heard what went over the air that over the air it was in this form:
The thought of horses on the payroll in the name of non-existent men-that was reported by Mr. Currie and hasn't been seriously challenged yet- that has been a cause of merriment, and understandably so.
This went over the air on Tuesday night, but I am convinced that it had been recorded for broadcast before the statement I had made in answer to the question of the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough), which I think would be taken as at least quite a serious challenge to the statement that there were horses on the payroll in the name of non-existent men. But I know from my own experience that frequently there are recordings made that go out over the air at the release hour or date.
That was his working paper.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Well, no; the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) suggests that the text was a working paper. It was a paper that was delivered to those who are interested in getting the text for release at the time the broadcast was made, while the working paper we have been discussing here was just about ten days prior to the date that the report was completed and signed, and actually delivered.
Unfortunately, however, many of those who heard the broadcast did not hear that there had been any answer to the question of the
*

Committee on Defence Expenditure
hon. member for Hamilton West as to what were the actual facts about the horse incident that had, understandably, caused such merriment.
Now, with respect to the amendment suggested by the hon. member, Your Honour has said that this is a direction which would be in order. It certainly appears to be a direction to the committee to do something that they would have the right to do without being directed to do it, and therefore something within the ruling you had previously made. But in view of all the facts which surround the Currie report at this time, I feel that the committee should be left to its own good judgment as to what it might or might not do in that connection, after it will have had an opportunity of hearing the witnesses, including Mr. Currie himself. And, though it is in order, I propose to register my vote against the hon. member's amendment, when we reach the appropriate time to do so.

Mr. Speaker, we in this group pressed for many years to have the committee on defence expenditures set up. We spoke in favour of it last year, and we are glad to see it set up again this year. During the last session I think the committee did a great deal of extremely valuable work. But all we did in that committee was to learn something about the organization of the armed forces, and to obtain a background for work to come.
I feel now that the committee is ready to proceed with its investigations into the realm of defence expenditures, to look into the entire field and to come forward with some mighty valuable results. To date we have not actually investigated to any great extent in regard to the actual defence expenditures. But if the committee set up this year works fearlessly and without thought of political affiliation, if it works without thought of endangering the stand of any party, then I think we can make an extremely valuable contribution, and one that will reflect great credit upon the members who comprise the committee.
I am not going to say much about the contents of the Currie report. We put our position quite clearly last fall with respect to it. I would repeat at this time that at no time have we put the blame on the shoulders of the army, but rather we feel that the blame for the entire situation lies with the administration of the Department of National Defence. We do condemn the government for not paying strict enough attention to the spending of the taxpayer's dollar in this regard. We find that today we labour under a tax structure which bears a ratio of five 6810S-65J
to one with that of 1939. The people's savings are beginning to become pretty well depleted. The dollar has devaluated to the point where people are having difficulty in meeting their bills. The least they can expect is full value for the defence dollar.
Canadians are entitled to and are demanding that we have strict honesty, maximum efficiency and maximum economy in the carrying out of our defence program. In this connection I should like to place on record part of an editorial from a recent edition of the Calgary Albertan. This is what it says:
The armed forces are notoriously wasteful and inefficient and apparently not much can be done about it. But unless there is an effort to control it, it can get completely out of hand. That's what happened here. There was no effort to control it. Certain senior officers must take immediate responsibility, but ultimately the defence minister, Mr. Claxton, must answer to the people.
I take it that this editorial refers only to the administration and the accounting in the army, and not to its ability in action. All hon. members know about the reputation and the ability of our army. Last fall the Acting Minister of National Defence said that in their rush to get men to fill these positions they had to take the good, bad and indifferent. I agree with him. They got the good-and all the army, with very few exceptions, is good. They got the bad-yes, they got a few crooks, as is pointed out in the Currie report. They got the indifferent; and in my opinion the indifferent are the entire Department of National Defence.
The acting minister said further that we had a shortage of staff, and the other day the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) reiterated that statement. If that is true, why were they so eager to let out so many civilian employees and so many of the personnel of the armed forces, when they knew that a dangerous condition might arise, and that these people might be needed in the near future?
Then, too, if they want to know where to get some men, perhaps they could borrow them from the Department of National Revenue; because some of the so-called little Hitlers who are running around the country checking up on people for their income tax returns might do a mighty good job digging into what is done in the Department of National Defence. And if they are half as good as some of them think they are, then that is the place for them.
Last fall the acting minister made reference to a bank robbery, and said that if a bank were robbed the president was not held to blame. But if the president left the money out on the sidewalk he would be to blame. And we find a similar situation in this
1028	HOUSE OF
Committee on Defence Expenditure instance, because the goods in question were left in the open, with no security measures being observed. They were just asking to be picked up by these people who are described as crooks.
He said, too, that if there were shortages, or that if there was embezzlement within a bank, the employees involved, and not the bank manager, had to pay the shot. The same reply could be made again, that if, through his lack of management, the bank manager made embezzlement possible, then he would be at fault and would be blamed accordingly. Not only that; if a report were made on that particular bank and those findings were made public, they certainly would not be turned over to the bank manager first for his O.K. and correction before being given out. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) may feel, from the fact that he asked Mr. Currie to make this investigation, that he was justified in asking for the report before it was presented to parliament. I also agree that it would be regrettable if there were any mention in the report of the young chap who was acquitted. I also should not like to see R.C.M.P. records put in such a report; but the fault in that regard lies with the minister because when he turned over the job to Mr. Currie he should have made clear what he wanted and did not want in the report. We do not like getting a watered-down report like this one in the House of Commons.
I noticed that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) today called the papers in the hands of the leader of the C.C.F. (Mr. Coldwell), working papers. That is the first time that expression has been used in the house. It is a happy thought devised by someone in the government in order to make appear less objectionable the actions of the minister in putting pressure on Mr. Currie to force him to make certain changes in the report before it was signed and delivered.
That brings me to the subamendment. Mr. Currie was appointed to investigate, and made his report. The minister intimated yesterday that the report was of very little value. In the letter of the minister which was accidentally placed on Hansard, and which I understand actually was not sent, the minister told Mr. Currie that. It certainly gives the minister's viewpoint on it.
The fact that Mr. Currie did yield to pressure has caused members of the house to lose a lot of confidence in him. Unlike the Minister of National Defence, we feel the report has been an extremely valuable contribution but we regret that Mr. Currie allowed himself to be intimidated. Therefore

in the opinion of this group Mr. Currie's usefulness is pretty well at an end because, for entirely different reasons, he has lost the confidence of members on both sides of the house. We cannot support the subamendment which asks that Mr. Currie be requested to continue and investigate the entire defence structure. We feel instead that a judicial inquiry should be carried on. We believe that a royal commission should be appointed to dig into the defence set-up, including contracts, buildings and everything else relating to defence and defence construction, and that a report should be made to the house as quickly as possible.
Coming to the amendment moved by the minister, he said yesterday that the loss, which was somewhere in the neighbourhood of $50,000, was practically negligible when compared with the total expenditure. If that is so and he feels that these losses are of little consequence, why does he insist on the defence expenditure committee looking into the matter first before investigating anything else? Mr. Currie pointed out that there were irregularities. They have been investigated and some of his recommendations have been carried out. The losses incurred have been made known. In my opinion the report has served its purpose.
Mr. Speaker, in view of the minister's statement on the report and his reference to Mr. Currie, and the fact that any political damage which could be done by the report has been done, I wonder whether or not this could be a move to keep the committee from digging into further defence expenditures, investigations which might be embarrassing.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That would not be according to the facts. Read the reference before the house and you will see that it covers all expenditures.
Then we had better let the committee get at the facts.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, order.

Mr. Speaker, I was amazed that the Minister of National Defence would move such an amendment to the motion; first, because it has never been done; second, it would appear to me that it is an indication of lack of faith in the ability of the committee; and third, as I said before, it might be interpreted as a means of bogging down the committee in work which has already been hashed over.
I just want to say one word about the report and the criticisms issued by the chief of the general staff. Many of the points covered by the Prime Minister this afternoon were well taken, but I sometimes

wonder whether or not the request that the members of the armed forces should not talk on this subject might come as the result of a fear that people might learn something that he did not want them to learn. I also wonder just how far the chief of the general staff would go and how long he would last if his statements, severe as they were, were contrary to rather than in favour of government policy. It seems to me rather strange that the chief of the general staff would instruct the men under him to keep silent but at the same time get up and speak himself. It is very much like the socialists; they always believe in socializing everyone but themselves, and it just does not make sense.
Keep to the Department of National Defence and never mind socialism.

I do not intend to take any further time of the house, but I do want to say that in my opinion this whole thing is another indication of the total disregard this government has for parliament, for parliamentary procedure and for the people whom these members represent.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, I have been in this house for almost thirteen years, and I must say that in those years nothing has ever happened to equal what took place this afternoon. I cannot understand the attitude of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in charging a member of this house with one of the most serious criminal offences with which a member can be charged and then finally, having made that charge-unwithdrawn-having recourse to the explanation that he believed that that was a fact.
This is a sorry day for parliament-for the preservation of this institution where, in the discussion of public affairs, however heated we may become on occasion, the maintenance of the proprieties must at all times be upheld and meticulously observed, not only by private members but by the Prime Minister as well, whose rights are no greater than those of any private member in the House of Commons.
Hear, hear.
I should add that I hold no brief for those who have done wrong, and if wrong has been done it should be punished.
Hear, hear.

I see the Prime Minister coming in now so I am going to repeat what I have said. In all my experience in the House of Commons, having seen him through the
Committee on Defence Expenditure years observing those proprieties without which parliament cannot be preserved, this afternoon was an occasion the memory of which I can only hope the years will erase. The Prime Minister charged a member of the House of Commons with a serious criminal offence, with no more proof to date than an investigation. I say to the Prime Minister that trials do not take place in the House of Commons. They still remain in the courts. I am disturbed by what the Prime Minister did this afternoon. I think he did it in one of those moments of very great annoyance when discretion leaves as annoyance mounts.
1 know nothing of the story connected with the migrations of the document and how it passed from hand to hand. However, my mind goes back, sir, to 1949 when the Prime Minister, speaking in the city of Regina, said there was only one difference between Liberals and C.C.F.-that the C.C.F. were Liberals in a hurry. That might be an explanation of the reason they acquired the document before it came officially to the notice of the house.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: That is the best part of your speech so far.

This afternoon I am not going to be sidetracked into dealing with the army and the responsibilities of the C.C.F. for getting possession of documents before parliament had them, however embarrassing those documents may be to the government. After all, the issue is-and I say this to the Prime Minister-what are you going to do about this? The Canadian people today, taxed as never before, are not asking us to fight sham battles in the House of Commons or to raise smokescreens regarding circumstances under which documents came to the public gaze. What they are asking the government of this country is to see to it that for every dollar spent for defence a dollar in value will be secured, and that waste and extravagance will end.
One of the things the Currie report did was to give proof, and final proof, of many of the allegations made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) and those associated with him, many of them soldiers distinguished in war. Over the years they have stated in this house that waste and extravagance existed in this country. The government intends to do nothing, having appointed Mr. Currie and having placed on his head the halo of all perfections, but set up a committee in parliament with a large and overwhelming majority of Liberal members to determine whether the investigator came to the right conclusion.
That is a strange procedure. I know that on occasions-and I am sure this applies to

Committee on Defence Expenditure the Prime Minister-having had a case tried as Currie tried this case and being dissatisfied, being on the losing side, I would have liked nothing better than to get together with the judge or, in the absence of the judge, friends of the losing litigant to review the findings of the judge in order to make them more palatable. That is exactly what is being done by the motion before the house. I thought that today the Prime Minister would stand up in his place and, instead of giving us a lecture on how parliament should act, do something such as was done during the first world war when there was wrongdoing. The prime minister of that day did not ask that the committee of parliament to be set up should be overwhelmingly Conservative. What he asked was that the public accounts committee be set up, and that it go to work and bring in, unfettered by any consideration, the truth as the truth was revealed.
I have before me the debates of that time. I enjoin the Prime Minister even yet to follow that example in setting up this committee. Committees of parliament heretofore in dealing with controversial matters have never shown that independence of their master's voice that is to be expected in a committee that is to review the review made by Mr. Currie, the appointed representative of the government. In 1915, when the public accounts committee was convened, Right Hon. Sir Robert Borden gave these instructions through a representative to the committee and the committee acted on them. I quote from page 2604 of Hansard for April 15, 1915:
I want to say that if there is any information the committee want, or any wrongdoing, then as far as the government is concerned we want to ferret it right to the bottom; we do not want to shield any person.
Later on he said:
The government is determined to protect fully the interests of the country in this and in all cases and to take such proceedings as may be necessary for that purpose. I want to repeat here again that so far as this government is concerned they want to prosecute their investigation to the very utmost limit.
Again, on another occasion:
As representing the government I have stated that we want to get to the bottom of these matters.
With those instructions from the Prime Minister and his representative, the committee met and brought forth evidence of wrongdoing. It exposed wrongdoing instead of adopting the attitude that is being adopted in this case, of trying to have a committee set up in order to review the findings of the umpire appointed by the government, dissatisfied with those findings.
