I was amazed at the statement the Prime Minister made this afternoon. Just as a


matter of information, I asked him when the army would be able to talk about the Currie report, when the ban against free speech in the army would be removed. The answer he gave was in effect that he presumed it would be after the committee had reported on the report. That is a new type of freedom of speech, the right of the men in the armed forces to voice their opinions on the Currie report after the government has taken that report and put it through the whitewash of a committee which is apparently being set up for that purpose. No, Mr. Speaker, you cannot erase the words of that Currie report. I believe it is in the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam that it is written:
The moving finger writes; and, having writ, Moves on: nor all your piety nor wit Shall lure it back to cancel half a line,
Nor all your tears wash out a word of it.
The Currie report stands as one of the greatest indictments of a government ever rendered, for its failure to discover waste and extravagance. It supports the stand taken by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes), by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) and the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness). Every time they brought this matter before parliament they were ridiculed. Now the report tells the story.
A rewrite job cannot remove the findings made in that report. It provides the final proof of what Canadians have suspected and have been speaking about from one end of the country to the other, that there is waste, extravagance and negligence of the government in the administration of expenditures for our defence, not only in Petawawa camp but elsewhere. It is not the army that is responsible, and it is not my hon. friends to the left who have the unexpurgated working papers. The responsibility rests upon the government of this country and upon the Prime Minister. It is not discharged by him by reading a lecture to the house or placing himself, as it were, above these things, as if grandchildren were acting rather naughtily without his knowledge.
Today, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister had an opportunity of making a declaration that where wrongdoing existed-not the petty thievery to which he referred, but where waste and extravagance existed-it would be eradicated. Instead of taking such a stand, a stand which would have won the keen admiration of the members of this house and of the people of this country, he took it upon himself to devote his time to certain things-if they are wrong that has yet to be established-which in no way afford an escape-hatch to the government for its failure to carry out the responsibilities that it must

carry out. When Canadians are being taxed at the highest level in Canadian history, surely they have a right to ask that the attitude of the government will not be that of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) -"What is a million anyhow?"-or the recent attitude of the Prime Minister following a suggestion by one of the members of the opposition-". . . that would be only a $3 million saving". The government may set up a committee, and the committee may act as it would act if it were directed, but it cannot remove these two portions of the report which read as follows:
The conclusion I have come to is that, while there has been a general breakdown in the system of administration, supervision and accounting, it was only at Petawawa that extensive irregularities over a prolonged period of time took place.
Those are the words concerning a general breakdown. Where is there anything of hope for the Canadian people in the message of the Prime Minister today? Calumny of political opponents cannot answer what the Canadian people are asking us in this parliament to do, to end waste and extravagance, realizing that our defence problem will possibly last for generations. Surely the taxpayers of Canada have the right to ask that they be relieved, by the practice of the luxury of denial of waste and extravagance on the part of the government, so they may look forward to reductions in taxation; and by that I do not mean cyclical reductions where the cycle comes around just prior to an election. On the same page of the report, negligence and downright stupidity are revealed in these words:
-it must be said that internal warnings had not been lacking in the Department of National Defence. The chief auditor of the department had performed his functions conscientiously. Time and again he had reported unsatisfactory conditions. This is clear from appendix "B" which summarizes his findings over a period of years.
Carelessness is nothing recent; it has continued over a period of years. The report continues:
The deputy minister in each case had directed the quartermaster general to investigate and report. Lack of adequate action at this point had, however, caused a progressive deterioration in the situation. Aside from reports being delayed for considerable periods of time, the record shows the next audit revealing conditions similar to those previously reported and, in some cases, worse. The process is then again repeated.
If ever there was an indictment of a department, surely that is one. I am glad to note that the minister said he is not looking for any scapegoats. As far as I am concerned we have had enough animals in this matter without a scapegoat. No minister need become a scapegoat. The responsibility is that of the government and of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), and it cannot be
Committee on Defence Expenditure discharged by placing the responsibility or the blame on the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) alone.
Then, at pages 715 and 716 the report continues:
There was in addition a serious collapse in security. There was little to prevent or to detect the organized plundering of military stores on a systematic scale, although apparently comparatively little of it took place. If there is excuse for inefficient accounting, there is none for the failure of security which is, after all, a prime military consideration. I take a serious view of this breakdown. If it is easy to pilfer military stores, then, by the same token, it is easy to sabotage military equipment.
Then again, a little later on:
As mentioned earlier, I consider the security measures in force at Petawawa and elsewhere inadequate.
In other words the condemnation extends to lack of security at Petawawa and other camps. The responsibility for that rests upon the government of this country, and it is a responsibility that is not discharged by the setting up of a committee to ascertain whether or not it will be possible to secure a report that will consist of a varnish or an embroidery of wrongdoing instead of a demand on the part of the Prime Minister and his cabinet that this kind of thing must end.
Yes, we are "spending ourselves to destruction." That is what Lenin said. One of the hopes of communism is that in raising our material defences we shall so continue as to weaken our defences of the soul and of the spirit, that private enterprise will cease. When I look at the Canadian record of expenditure which is revealed again in the Currie report, 1 think it indicates, as we realized after Korea, that for the billions of dollars spent before that date we had little or nothing to show.
I think one of the records that has been established by this government is this. Never before have so many Canadians paid such high taxes for so little defence. That, in effect, sums up the record, Mr. Speaker. The report indicates that waste and extravagance have taken place. It also indicates that the road is one of uncontrolled spending and that, regardless of warnings given by spokesmen in the opposition on defence matters, by the hon. member for Nanaimo and others, the same conditions prevail in even exaggerated form. If some of the information that comes to members of parliament, and which has come to me, is in fact correct, it indicates that in the building of airports in this country waste is not one of those things that is being denied by careful accounting on the part of the government.
What is the government trying to do? They want to set up a committee. They make a microscopic examination with regard to

Committee on Defence Expenditure some of the mistakes that they say exist in the report. No amount of explanation with regard to horses can ever eradicate one thing and it is this. However they were there, there was in fact fraud connected with their being there; and no denial on the part of the government can answer the allegation that at Petawawa there was in fact a situation that has given to Canadians as a whole a horselaugh but at the same time a realization that if such things could exist, there is no limit to the extent to which waste and extravagance could go undetected.
We ask for action. The Canadian people are asking for action. They are asking for a reduction in taxation. Mr. Speaker, the byelections in the last two years have indicated clearly that the Canadian people have not that confidence in the government which the government has in the committee that it intends to set up to examine the report by Mr. Currie.
Rights of parliament? Mr. Speaker, no one wants wrongdoing. But the synthetic rage exhibited by the Prime Minister today will not give an answer to the Canadian people, to the question as to why it is that waste and extravagance exist. The people of Canada are beginning to realize why taxation is at its present high level. I am sure that if it continues much longer the Canadian people will be saying to the government what Cromwell once said: "You have sat too long here for any good you have been doing. Depart,
I say, and let us have done with you."
Mr. Speaker, the by-elections reveal the people's feelings. In 1935 Mr. King-and I have his speeches here-was answered by those then on the government benches in the same way: "We have a majority". His reply was in effect: "It is a phantom majority. It may be able to secure results now but it is no longer representative of the desire and the wishes of the Canadian people." I believe that today Canadians are not asking for smokescreens by the Prime Minister, and not for annoyances built up over the discovery of a document which, according to the Prime Minister, should not have been brought before parliament. What the people want to know of this government is this, and I come back to it because it is the subject in the minds and hearts of Canadians. Are you no longer qualified to meet the challenge to do away with waste and extravagance? Have you become all-powerful? Must a man like Pitt in Winnipeg be dismissed, or rather translated into other spheres because he did not show the respect to the members of the government, or to some of them, that those members believe they are entitled to? Have we come to a position in this country

where, regardless of what is being done, a committee is to be set up the purpose of which is as clear as one's hand in front of him? That purpose is to dissuade Canadians from believing in the integrity and the capacity of Mr. Currie who last March, April and May was pictured by members of the government as a man fitted in every way to discharge his responsibility with honour, with integrity and with responsibility.
What is the committee going to do? It is going to sit; it is going to review the Currie findings. Does anybody in this house suggest that those findings will not finally be diluted by the kind of examination that will take place? Will they not be given a gloss and a polish? Will the rough things not be removed, the elevations removed and the depressions filled in?
Why do you always ask for them?

Until that is done the Prime Minister says he believes it is fit and proper that the members of the armed forces of this country should not be permitted to discuss the matter. They are frightened; they are afraid to give any information any more. They are afraid to tell a member of parliament anything because if they do they place themselves in jeopardy. I am not speaking about this report now; I am speaking about the fact-and I say it to you, Mr. Speaker- that wherever one's parliamentary rights are interfered with each and every one of us has a responsibility, whatever our party, to oppose it. And if we come to a point where our sources of information are dried up by threat or fear of intimidation, then we are indeed placed in a position where wrong will be concealed, where the things that ought to be revealed will be kept under the kind of lid the Prime Minister and those associated with him believe will result from the setting up of this committee.
Members of parliament have no privileges to do wrong. Their privileges are restricted as they should be restricted. Indeed, our privileges are fewer than those of members of the British parliament. When approaching parliamentary buildings they have the right over approaching traffic, and are thereby preserved from potential injury. We do not have that here.
We can learn from the British parliament, and the quotations already given indicate above everything else that a principle is at stake, whatever the party may be, whoever the individual in parliament may be. The independence of members of parliament must

be maintained inviolate and not subject in any way to challenge unless a criminal offence is committed.
1 am not going to say anything about the answer of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson), but on several occasions when he has been asked "Why are you not doing something in that matter?" I have heard him say, in effect: "We cannot; the Attorney General of Canada dare not use the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Prosecutions under the Criminal Code are a matter for the attorney general of the province." I remember once he read me a lecture on the subject of the use of the police force. I am reminded too of the one he read to the house urging that appeals to the privy council should be abolished in order to remove colonialism from Canada; and he was the first one to appeal when he was dissatisfied with the judgment and secured one there that undermined the constitution.
I say this to him: He had no right to utilize the services of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police unless a charge had been preferred or an information laid, or unless the investigation was in pursuance of the attorney general's direction. I am pointing that out to him because I am quoting in effect the stand he has taken repeatedly.
Whatever happened in so far as that document is concerned, what annoys the government is that it was found out that the report brought before parliament had received treatment, the Lux treatment, in order to remove any stains on the government that may have been there. I sometimes wonder, Mr. Speaker, whether the reports we receive and the answers given in reply to parliamentary questions do not indicate that a similar form of treatment has been accorded them before being tabled in the House of Commons.
Parliament has its rights. Without parliament freedom cannot be maintained. Wrongdoing it will not condone. But parliament dare not allow its national police force to be used in any way that may be considered political, or to have a political purpose in mind. That is the most serious situation, as I see it, in connection with this matter. Using the mounted police-
National security.

-he being in need of information of a dependable character in that connection. As a matter of fact not one iota of national security is being undermined, not a suggestion of it, in any line of that entire report. But, Mr. Speaker, it does reveal in lurid colours, not in lurid words, a government spending without sufficient check billions of dollars and boasting about the surplus they have and the number of extra dollars they take out of every Canadian. They boast about their capacity to tax. What Canadians want them to be able to do is boast of their ability to assure that for every dollar spent there will be a dollar in defence, and not waste and extravagance.
They can do it, too.

They are doing it, too? I hope the Prime Minister puts my hon. friend on that committee, because he will be an unprejudiced member. Today I think the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) owed1 a duty to parliament not to endeavour to conceal, not to raise a smokescreen in order to cover up what the report reveals. What he should have done was come before parliament which, after all, is; based upon trust, and apologize to the Canadian people for having permitted conditions like this to exist, and instead of repudiating them when discovered, prosecuting only a few of those small wrongdoers. He should have given the assurance to parliament and the people of Canada that what has happened; is past, but that it will not happen again.
There was no such promise, no such undertaking. Instead of such an undertaking there is a motion for the setting up of a committee for the purpose-and I repeat this-of reviewing the findings of the man who, they said with all the power at their command, was a man that they would trust. Trust! And when he made a return they ordered him, they directed him-and this was without the Prime Minister's knowledge-to bring in the findings, the work sheets, to see whether the work he had done would meet with the approval of those whose responsibility it was to see that things like that did not occur. I say the time has come for parliament not to be setting up such committees.

That is news.

Committee on Defence Expenditure

Someone has said to me, "Well, some of your members have asked for committees of parliament." Yes, and I have asked for them in the past. But from the experience I have had, with the exception of the committee on external affairs, and in a lesser degree the committee on radio, as well as one or two others, the conclusions at which they arrived had all the spontaneity that a directed verdict from the government would demand.
That is not what the Canadian people want. Currie spoke as he saw the evidence revealed. He wrote it down in a report, and he made recommendations; but it was suggested that he remove some of those factual things that would shock the sensibilities of the government. When, the report is finally produced, and the government finds itself in a position of being indicted, it asks for the setting up of a committee, a jury of its own, to determine whether the judge came to the right conclusion.
Is there that degree of responsibility in an attitude of that kind that you, Mr. Speaker, as the custodian of the conscience of parliament, would expect? If Currie was what he was in March and April last, the epitome of propriety, a man of infinite capacity and integrity, why set up a committee in 1953, eight months later, for the purpose of ascertaining whether or not the conclusions he arrived at were, in fact, the proper ones?
We tried to move an amendment, but we did not succeed. Your Honour found that our amendment was not within the rules. When I heard the Prime Minister close his remarks today by saying that he would vote against having Mr. Currie continue with the investigation, I wondered why.

That he would vote against the amendment-and I thank my hon. friend for that interruption, because it indicates that he is in favour of Mr. Currie; but is going to vote against giving Canada an opportunity of using Mr. Currie's services to find wrongdoing where it exists, to reveal waste and extravagance wherever it may be found and, above everything else, to do what the Canadian people sent us here to do-to save them money and end this orgy of waste that is going on across the country, so as to assure Canadians a dollar's return for every dollar spent in defence.

Mr. Speaker, it would be very difficult for me, a


new and inexperienced member, to follow the dramatic oratory of the experienced parliamentarian from Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker). But throughout his speech I noted such a similarity to a speech of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), which I intend to quote in a few moments, that I do not think it necessary to pay further attention to what the hon. member said, any more than to point out that at the beginning and at the close of his most dramatic address he drew analogy between the Currie report and a case in court.
Of course no one is better qualified to draw that analogy, because the hon. member has a reputation well known in the courts. Yet he said that referring the Currie report to a committee was like calling in the judge and talking over the case. Well, I think the hon. member in his career has, on more than one occasion, known of cases referred to a court of appeal on some point. I think, sir, that if I had been sitting where he sits and had been making his speech, and he had been over here, he would have folded his arms and said, "Where, oh where, Mr. Speaker, is the principle of the grand old Tory party that parliament is always the final court of appeal?"
We are debating a resolution which asks- That a select committee be appointed to continue the examination of all expenditure of public moneys for national defence and all commitments for expenditure for national defence since March 31, 1950, and to report from time to time their observations and opinions thereon, and in particular, what, if any, economies consistent with the execution of the policy decided by the government may be effected therein.
And then the powers of the committee are set out. To this resolution an amendment and a subamendment have been moved, both of which tend either to guide or instruct the committee in the carrying out of that resolution.
I was a member of the committee that sat last year, and I presume the duties of this year's committee will be much the same, namely to investigate all expenditures for national defence. But it will be only natural that some priority will be given to those expenditures which have been made the subject of charges or criticisms against the government.
It is earnestly to be hoped that this year the charges and criticisms which will cause the committee a lot of work may be at least reasonably well founded. Last year I permitted myself to be quite impressed by a speech made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) who, I regret, is not in his seat at the moment. It was a good speech, well delivered. It was impressive and I, not

having the experience then that I have now, was quite impressed. He said, as found at page 1797 of Hansard for May 1 last year:
The Petawawa incident is something which does more than merely raise the necessity for charges being laid. It is a great deal more than that. Let us remember that this is not the first time that there have been extensive thefts from camps here in Canada. This is not the first time that there have been warnings to the Department of National Defence that it was necessary that there be careful supervision of the military establishments of this country. There was, for instance-apart from other lootings in other camps-the dramatic episode at Farnham in Quebec where, for all practical purposes, it was discovered in December, 1949, that a whole camp had disappeared. That camp was equipped with plumbing, electrical fixtures, wiring, sinks, showers, refrigerators and all the things that go along with camps . . . That camp disappeared except for a few of the walls and the foundations which could not be conveniently moved. Of more than 100 wooden structures-and very solid wooden structures they were-in that huge camp area, an undisclosed number had been lifted intact from their foundations by a heavy-tracked vehicle and sold for prices ranging from $25 to $50 to farmers and other residents in the eastern townships at that time.
I think perhaps I am to be forgiven for having been quite impressed by that charge, and I decided when I was made a member of the committee that I was going to find out about that one. Eventually we got to it. We did not get to it right at the start but finally we did, and you will find the proceedings with respect to it reported at page 246 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of last year's committee. The witness before the committee at the time was Mr. E. B. Armstrong, assistant deputy minister for finance, Department of National Defence. I shall have to weary the house with a few of the questions and answers. I was the questioner and Mr. Armstrong was the witness. They are:
Q. What is the total amount of our investment at Farnham when it was an operating camp?
A. The total investment at Farnham was $96,344.40.
Q. And that covered a camp of something over 200 buildings?
A. That covered a camp of something over 200 buildings, plus the services that went into the camp.
Q. And of these 200 buildings, thirty-one were stolen?
A. Of these 200 buildings thirty-one were stolen, yes.
Q. And twenty-six of those stolen were recovered?
A. Twenty-six of the thirty-one were recovered.
Q. The net loss in buildings was five, is that right?
A. That is right.	.

A. I beg your pardon?

So, Mr. Speaker, the Farnham bubble burst. The bombshell delivered so forcibly by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) in the house turned out to be not even a child's firecracker but a very wet and very defunct squib. Surely that justifies the wording of the editorial in the Ottawa Citizen of January 14 in which it is suggested that criticism should "be based on knowledge rather than on gossip and conjecture." Committee on Defence Expenditure here for many years, that more information was supplied to the defence expenditures committee last year than has been supplied to any committee of this house within the memory of these men. I know from personal experience that the volume of typed returns which came in as a result of the questions, and the detailed answers we got from the witnesses, were quite sufficient, had there been no other parliamentary business going on at the time, to keep the members of that committee fully occupied for ten or fourteen hours a day. Those members of the committee who sat there day in and day out, whether or not the subject under investigation was spectacular, will agree with the truth of what I have said.
I should like to refer to a speech made by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) on the radio program "The Nation's Business". I doubt if there is any member in the house who is accorded more general respect than the hon. member for Vancouver East. In this recent broadcast he made, as he always makes, an excellent speech. One may not always agree with everything he says, but you have to admit that he says it well and makes it sound very reasonable. In dealing with the Currie report he stressed the angle that the Currie report indicates a tendency toward a breakdown in security. I believe he has a point there. He pointed out with perfect justification that there are tremendously dangerous implications if in this country our security breaks down. I should like to say to the hon. member for Vancouver East, and to those of his party, that the security of this country is not likely to be enhanced so long as the mentality exists in Canada that the obtaining by any means or the retaining of unauthorized property is a legitimate or natural proceeding.
In the first half of his address the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) referred at considerable length to Mr. George Currie's discussions with the department. I am neither a member of that department nor very high in its confidence, so I do not know of what these discussions consisted. Undoubtedly the member for Winnipeg North Centre felt that such discussions should not have been held. I suppose the majority of the members of this house are or have been at some time the heads of some sort of organization, perhaps a law office with three or four employees or perhaps a large factory with 300 or 400 employees. I suggest that if any of them suspected that there was pilfering or a leak of some kind in their organization, they would call in a chartered accountant to investigate the matter. This


chartered' accountant would be working for them to find out the answers to the problems that were troubling them.
Are you going to tell me that one of these employers would not have the right to discuss his own problems with the auditor who was called in to assist him in solving those problems? Unless I have this thing all wrong, Mr. Speaker, the impression seems to be held by a great many people that the Currie investigation was a secret investigation of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) for this house. According to the way I look at it, it was an investigation for the Minister of National Defence. The minister asked for an investigation of his own organization. It seems to me that that auditor and the minister personally could conceivably and justifiably have gotten together every few days as the investigation went along, to find out how the thing was going along and to see if either could give any assistance or information to the other. Why not?
There is another aspect of the Currie report which I should like to mention briefly. May I hsk you to call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

Mr. Speaker, in replying to the comprehensive outline given by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), in which he quite frankly pointed out the shortage of manpower available when we were hit by the Korean conflict, the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) stated that the shortage of forces of any kind was due to this government's policy in approximately 1946 and 1947.
To that statement I do not think anybody can take any exception. But had this country been asked by this government in 1946 or 1947 to maintain a standing army-which is what it would have been-the size of that which we now have, I wonder what we would have heard from the opposition, and what criticisms we would have had as to adopting a military attitude, as to wasting the public funds, and so on and so forth, at a time when, let me remind you, the whole world was war-sick and peace-minded, and when disarmament was practically the keynote of the policies of all the democracies.
Oh, yes, they may say, but what about Russia? This is a fine example of one particular attribute which the opposition has in

unlimited quantities, namely a comprehensive hindsight. Mr. Churchill, Mr. Truman nor any of the other great leaders of that day in the world were able to foresee the situation in which we find ourselves today. However, the hon. member for Nanaimo does not always make statements with which I disagree. In the course of his speech, as reported at page 961 of Hansard, he said:
It is for the government to defend itself and to explain how it has taken care of the $2 billion of the taxpayers' money which this department has been called upon to expend in the cause of national defence.
With that statement I entirely agree. It is for this government to account for those expenditures, and that is exactly what this committee is being set up for. As to the hon. member's criticism of the make-up of the committee, I had already dealt with that matter before the supper recess. But if he is against such a committee, if he is against this government making its defence before a committee appointed by this parliament, where are all these Conservative claims for the supremacy of parliament? Where have they gone? The hon. gentleman's real complaint is not the appointment of this committee. His real complaint is the verdict which was rendered by the electorate in 1949, as a result of which we find ourselves with the set-up we have today. He admitted that plaintively and I quote his own words as reported at page 964 of Hansard:
Therefore if the representatives of the Conservatives and the other groups all voted together they were only able to marshal nine votes against the seventeen of the supporters of the government on the committee.
It is perhaps tragic from the hon. member's point of view, but that is the situation; and it would be a much more exaggerated situation were the defence to be made in detail in this house instead of in a committee appointed by this house.
The hon. gentleman suggests that what is needed now is not more committees but action on the report. In that connection he read into the record a letter written by his own leader which stated in part:
You said that the Currie report would be submitted to the committee on defence expenditures. One of my reasons for writing this letter is to point out that this procedure is neither necessary nor desirable.
And further on:
We need no inquiry into the report of another inquiry. We need action on the report now before us. It makes positive recommendations.
For once the official opposition does not want action by a committee, for the first time in its history. It says it wants action on the report. It has got it. The minister
Committee on Defence Expenditure has already outlined that. It has got action on most of the recommendations, most of which were implemented before they were even made. The hon. member for Nanaimo complains because the department is, to use his own words, "resentful of criticism". As reported at page 964 of Hansard he said:
This department is following the pattern set up by the government. It is resentful of any criticism which may be offered of it.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) seems to agree. It seems to me that these opposition members are resentful of any effort to straighten out the record in the face of the wild charges which have been made by some of the opposition members. They also appear to me to be resentful of anyone's defending himself against any charge which they may see fit to make.
If I may, I should like to turn my attention for a moment to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who is in his seat and who-it should be said, to be fair-is always in his seat except when he is on his feet. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who has been the one all through this incident to take the lead in bringing before the house the mysterious unauthorized copy of the Currie report, seems to me to have adopted the attitude of the young man who tosses a coin in the air and confidently expects it to come down both heads and tails. As reported at page 972 of Hansard, he stated:
The report that came into the possession of my leader was not covered by any official secrets act. It was not a government document.
He said on page 968:
Between the first draft and the second draft changes were made.
He complained earlier, on page 655:
I have since had an opportunity, which I had not had at the time I asked my question this morning, to compare some of the pages in the printed report which was tabled this morning with the same pages in another printed copy of the report which has been in our possession for a few days.
Either it is or it is not a report which was the property of the Department of National Defence. How can they justify their criticism of the supposed changes in the report if it was not a government report; and how can they object to, shall we say, conjecture from this side of the house as to how it came into their possession; if it was a copy of a confidential report which was then to be, but had not yet been submitted to the minister, is not there some justification perhaps for our feelings of criticism?
I hope this committee, as the resolution says, continues with its investigation. Even the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes)

Committee on Defence Expenditure admitted in the beginning of his remarks that last year the committee did accomplish some beneficial results. It can accomplish a lot more. It can accomplish those results only after it has been set up and has been put to work. I should like to see that done at the earliest possible moment, and I would express the hope that when it has been constituted the Liberal members appointed thereto will be looking for facts and not for headlines.

Mr. Speaker, the tabling of the Currie report in this House of Commons on December 15 was a major event in current Canadian political history; and whatever has been said since, as this issue has moved from one climax to another, will never subtract one iota from the importance of that event.
I wish to go back, however, to events that occurred in the week prior to the tabling of the report in this house. This story was unfolded to us by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in the statement he made several weeks ago. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) was absent on duty in Paris, and the report came into the hands of the Acting Minister of National Defence, the Solicitor General (Mr. Campney), we were told, on December 9, as he was departing for Toronto, catching a train. Now, it is interesting to follow up this important mission upon which the Solicitor General was embarking at the time this report was placed in his possession. Was it an event of great national importance that took him away from the capital at the moment this report was placed in his hands as Acting Minister of National Defence? Actually the mission the Solicitor General was embarking on as he took his train for Toronto on that occasion was to address a certain Liberal group which met the following day, and in the course of his address to that political group-

speechtext: What is wrong with that?

There is this wrong with it: The tabling of this report in the house was delayed at least a couple of days by reason of the fact that the minister concerned was more involved at the moment in fulfilling some partisan engagement than he was in attending to the nation's business; that is all.
Now, what did the minister have to say on this occasion in addressing this particular meeting?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: May I just say that I stated very clearly that the reason the tabling of the report was delayed was in order that it might first be put in the hands of the Prime Minister, and of the Minister of National Defence. The event to which my hon. friend refers had nothing to do with it.

The only thing that is wrong with the hon. gentleman's reply is that it does not jibe with the record as we have been told of the events. But let me go on to what was said on the important mission that took the minister away, when there was no time to consider the Currie report. He is reported in the Toronto Daily Star of Tuesday, December 9, as having said to those he was addressing:
But let us, above all, tell the people of this country what we have done.
Further down in the article he speaks of "Canada's fine contribution to collective defence, and the complete freedom from graft or scandal in the national government."
Hear, hear.

And, Mr. Speaker, the minister had in his possession at that time the Currie report which exposed the greatest national scandal in this country since the Beauharnois scandal was exposed by Mr. Bennett twenty years ago. Here we have a typical example of Liberal propaganda, the minister leaving this report behind in Ottawa and apparently not having time to read it, and making a statement which is so completely contradicted by the facts that were then available.
Now, sir, it is no wonder that there is so much confusion on the part of hon. members to your right, Mr. Speaker, in connection with this whole matter, because there has been hopeless confusion in the government's approach to it ever since the Currie report was tabled in this house. A variety of contradictions and confusion on their part is nothing new. We who sit in this house see it opposite continually, but on this occasion it was perhaps a little more marked because variety apparently was unlimited.
The first approach by the government members of this house was reflected in a speech made on December 16 by the hon. member for Northumberland, Ont. (Mr. Robertson), who apparently went out of his way to seek to put the blame on the "top brass". Then you remember that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) spoke in the house on the same day. He was met by a chorus of interruptions by hon. members opposite, who sometimes find that about the only way they have to participate in proceedings, in which they kept shouting about the "top brass". That apparently was the way the matter stood at that time. The idea, the strategy of the government-at least of its followers-at that time was to place responsibility on those who are called the top brass.

Then you remember, Mr. Speaker, how significant it was that in the discussion of a matter of such vital national importance the Prime Minister remained silent. There was plenty of opportunity for him to participate but when it came to putting up a minister on Wednesday evening, December 17, to make the first statement on behalf of the government, in the absence of the Minister of National Defence, who was it that should have made that statement? I submit to you, sir, the statement should have been made by the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister did not make the statement. He put up instead the junior member of the cabinet-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

-a man who had no responsibility for events that are referred to in the report. He was not a member of the cabinet at that time. He had been a member of the cabinet for only a few days. I do not think it was fair to the Solicitor General to put him in that position at that time. It was, in my submission, the responsibility of the Prime Minister; but that responsibility was not discharged.
The next stage, Mr. Speaker, was the statement made by the Solicitor General on the evening of December 17, and it was very interesting. What was his approach to the question? It became obvious at once, because the minister had not gone any more than a matter of several minutes before he struck the key note, and it was this: The whole matter of the Currie report was, as he put it, "a relatively small matter". Further on in his remarks he said: "in the aggregate it is not of very great magnitude". Further on he complained about the exaggeration of the opposition, although everything we had said had been drawn directly from the text of the report.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we had an opportunity of gauging the government's approach at that stage. The attempt at that point was to play down the report, to minimize it, to make it appear that after all it was a trifling matter, and it was nothing for anybody in the country or in parliament to get very much excited about.
Well, it was not to be expected that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) would be silent very long, and he turned up at Kingston the following Saturday night and made a statement there. It is reported in the Toronto Daily Star of December 20-

That is all old stuff.

I think it is high time the hon. member had his memory refreshed on some of these things. I know he does not like being reminded of some of these silly statements the ministers are making as they flit around the country, but he is going to hear one or two more if he stays in the house. Here is what the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) said about the Currie report:
But I also think Mr. Currie, as a professional man, was rather extravagant with some of his statements, when all he was supposed to do was report on facts and suggest improvements.
Apparently Mr. Currie, in the view of the strong man of the cabinet, has committed the cardinal offence of going outside what he was supposed to do. Apparently in passing some words of judgment, for which the Canadian people ought to be grateful to Mr. Currie, he did something he was not supposed to do; and therefore he has come under the censure of the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
Then, of course, come the things which occurred during the Christmas recess. The Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair), out at the coast, referred to the report as "threshing old straw". The Solicitor General (Mr. Campney), becoming vocal again, talked about exaggeration, and said that the report would "not cut much ice". I think every hon. member will find out that if the report does not cut much ice, it will at least fan the fires of indignation on the part of the Canadian people against this government for its hopeless inefficiency.
Now the Solicitor General has again become vocal, and on this occasion in Toronto. He is reported in the morning press of that city as having said last night in a speech to the Davenport Liberal association:
The Currie report has ballooned out of all proportion to its importance.
And then he said further:
In a business as big as defence is today, there would always be untrustworthy people. They are no more numerous at Petawawa than in any other large business.
And then this significant statement appears:
The Currie report, said Mr. Campney, is an exposure of normal thieving.
Oh, oh.

And then:
"Nobody is pleased about thieving, but you can't stop people from stealing".
So we have it summed up that what went on at Petawawa was merely normal thieving; and apparently it became normal because it took place under a government which has proven itself so hopelessly inefficient in stopping it. That is the measure of the normalcy.

Committee on Defence Expenditure
May I ask the hon. member a question?

I would ask the hon. member to reserve his question until later.
Then we had the statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) today. At last the Prime Minister was drawn into this debate-at last. With every indication of reluctance he was drawn into it. He said if it had not been for some statements made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) he would not have participated in this debate. Well, why not? Is this debate so relatively unimportant that the Prime Minister thinks it is beneath him to participate in it? I say this: More power to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre if he was responsible for, shall we say, drawing or luring the Prime Minister into this debate. And I suppose, Mr. Speaker, that reluctance on the part of the Prime Minister is all part of the government's tactics to play down this report and picture it as something very unimportant, something to be minimized.
There are two major issues which have emerged in the discussions of the Currie report, both of which, in my submission, are of the highest importance to the Canadian parliament. The first has to do with the importance of the report, and the second has to do with responsibility.
As to the importance of the report, the confusion of the government was climaxed when the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) used these words here two days ago in reference to the report: "this important document". At long last we have a minister who says this document is important. This is the report that other members of the government, including the Acting Minister of National Defence, were saying was a relatively unimportant matter. Now finally, the Minister of National Defence has corrected the minister who was acting in his absence, and who had referred to the contents of the report as a relatively small matter.
Again, the Minister of National Defence said, and) very properly, in his speech in the house two days ago that he did not want anybody to consider that he thought what has happened at Petawawa was not serious. Well, that may be a guarded admission; but at any rate we have a minister who seems to say it is serious, and who makes the statement that this Currie report is an important document-and this in the face of statements directly to the contrary by other ministers. In the second place there is an admission on the part of the minister that what happened
{Mr. Fleming.]

at Petawawa is serious-and this after other ministers have been saying that it is a matter of no great magnitude.
That admission by the Minister of National Defence, sir, really was not necessary, because the country well knows how important this matter is. The country has attached a great deal of importance to the Currie report and the shocking scandals which have been exposed by it. And I say that no amount of denial or propaganda or gainsaying or cajolery on the part of ministers or government followers will ever minimize the importance of this report. It has, indeed, revealed the worst scandal in the affairs of government since the Beauharnois scandal was exposed twenty years ago. Make no mistake about it, it has shocked the Canadian people. It has shocked the Canadian conscience.
The other important subject, I said, was that of responsibility. And so I go back to a statement made by the Prime Minister when he spoke in the debate on the address in reply on November 24 when, making reference to the subject of fires and thefts and extravagance in the Department of National Defence, he had this to say:
Much is made of the few regrettable incidents having to do with thefts which have occurred in camps, having to do with fires which have broken out in camps, and incidents of that nature. These are deplorable; but has anyone tried to hold the presidents of the banks responsible because the Boyd gang broke into and robbed the banks? Has anyone attempted to hold a high official of the Bank of Nova Scotia responsible because there is a report that that bank was successfully defrauded of the sum of $250,000 recently?
Mr. Speaker, that of course was uttered before the Currie report had been handed to the government. But it was uttered with reference to a directly comparable matter; and the Prime Minister was taking great care, in public, to wash his hands of personal responsibility, or of governmental responsibility, for anything in the nature of fire, thefts and extravagance within the Department of National Defence.
That has been the tone set throughout the debate; at least it was until two days ago. There has been a denial of responsibility by the Prime Minister, a denial of governmental responsibility, notwithstanding that the institution in which we are meeting this day owes its existence and its dignity to the fact that parliament looks to the government collectively to be responsible for what happens in departments of government entrusted to the charge of ministers.
Well, the Minister of National Defence very properly in his speech two days ago said that he took full responsibility for what happened in his department. That is the

first time any minister or government spokesman has said such a thing since the Currie report was tabled. Other statements have been directed toward a denial of government responsibility.
And, sir, now that the minister has accepted responsibility, under the principle of collective responsibility the whole cabinet bears the responsibility for what has happened. In retaining the minister, the government shares full responsibility with him, and in equal measure. And let me say this to the Liberal majority in the house, that in now retaining in office a government which shares full responsibility for what has happened, that Liberal majority in the house now shares the responsibility of the government for permitting it to continue in office.
The speech made by the Minister of National Defence two days ago was an interesting if not too impressive attempt to explain away the report, its recommendations, its criticisms and its exposures. It was no light paintbrush that he applied. Had one not known the background, and been a complete stranger to the issue before coming into the house, one would have had the feeling that he should have cheered the minister and expressed gratitude to him that things were not very much worse than they were.
That's for sure.

I can tell hon. members opposite that the attempts that have been made by ministers and government supporters in this debate this week to deliver attacks on the Currie report-and not always frontal attacks, but rather stealthy attacks-are not going to have the effect of discrediting either Mr. Currie or the report he has written, and in the writing of which he has performed' a service to the Canadian people of the highest magnitude. Yes, any attempt to wash the horses out of the report will only call to mind the fact that that, as we have been told now by the Minister of National Defence, was one of the matters the deputy minister of national defence took up with Mr. Currie and invited him, before his report was submitted to the government, to eliminate from the report. Mr. Currie stood by his statement that horses were placed on the payroll under the names of non-existent labourers.
Horselaughs.

Mr. Currie stands by that, and I think we will want more than statements obtained by the government from a convict now serving a penitentiary term to convince us that Mr. Currie was wrong in the statements he made and by which he stuck.
Committee on Defence Expenditure
Now the government is stuck.
You are stuck right now.

It will not serve, either, Mr. Speaker, to reduce the long list of reprehensible and scandalous practices that are revealed in the report, quite apart from horses entirely. The shortcomings of the Department of National Defence, as exposed in the report, are summed up by Mr. Currie in the expressions, and I am quoting his own language: "general breakdown in the system of administration", "lax control, poor discipline and presence of dishonest personnel.	The combination proved disastrous"; "a fundamentally loose situation", "the accounting records were in a chaotic condition", "a serious collapse in security". Are these the matters which the government now invites us and the Canadian people to gloss over and consider to be of little or no importance?
No, Mr. Speaker, it will take a great deal more to satisfy the conscience of the Canadian people, in the face of these exposures by an eminently capable investigator, than the kind of statements we have been hearing from the ministers. Let it not be forgotten, sir, that warnings were plentiful. This whole investigation was started, if you please, as the outcome of the receipt of an anonymous letter, but Mr. Currie has been at pains to point out that previous warnings had been numerous. He had this to say, as found at page 712 of Hansard:
-it must be said that internal warnings had not been lacking in the Department of National Defence. The chief auditor of the department had performed his functions conscientiously. Time and again he had reported unsatisfactory conditions. This is clear from Appendix "B" which summarizes his findings over a period of years. The deputy minister in each case had directed the quartermaster general to investigate and report. Lack of adequate action at this point had, however, caused a progressive deterioration in the situation. Aside from reports being delayed for considerable periods of time, the record shows the next audit revealing conditions similar to those previously reported and, in some cases, worse. The process is then again repeated.
What did the deputy minister of national defence do when what he had done in calling these reports of the chief auditor to the attention of the quartermaster general had been ignored? Apparently he did nothing further. What did the minister at the head of that department do? Well, sir, it remains yet to be told to the house whether the minister was aware of these reports of the chief auditor of his department. I hope the minister will tell the house some time before this debate concludes whether he was aware of the reports of the chief auditor of the department to which reference is made in

Committee on Defence Expenditure the paragraph I have just read. If he was not aware of these reports being currently received, then why did he not know? Why, as the responsible head of the department, did he not make it his business to be acquainted with important reports submitted by the chief auditor of the department? If he did know, then why did he not direct that action be taken promptly?
We are hearing now about government willingness to take action promptly when a situation arises. What about these precious months-yes, years-that have gone by when no action whatever was taken? Hon. members will not have forgotten that in the defence expenditure committee last year reference was made, as appears at page 173 of the proceedings, to reports that were being sent in to the department running back, if you please, to June 2, 1949. There were about a dozen of these reports. Was the minister aware of them? If he was not aware of them why was he not? If he was aware of them, why was action not taken to deal with the scandalous conditions they exposed?
Then there is the question of extent. The Solicitor General (Mr. Campney) went to great pains to play down the matter as one of not very great importance in the aggregate. That is not what Mr. Currie says. Mr. Currie puts a very different complexion upon the facts. As found at page 714 of Hansard, he says, after referring to the catalogue or enumeration of some of these scandals and irregularities:
These, then, represent the ascertained cases of irregularity at Petawawa. How many more there may have been will never be known. It was apparent from the beginning of the investigation that the accounting records were in a chaotic condition and would be of little use in determining the nature and extent of irregularities. It is impractical and perhaps impossible, regardless of the time which might be spent on examining records, to try and determine by this means the amount and value of the deficiencies.
He did not stop there, because in the following column he went on to say:
My view would be, however, that the generally lax administrative situation would give rise to waste and inefficiency far more costly in loss than that covered by actual dishonesty.
When the Solicitor General flits about the country making political speeches before partisan audiences and says that it is a small matter in the aggregate, involving not more than $50,000, I confront him with the statement of Mr. Currie that the loss cannot be measured and in any event, even if the loss could be ascertained, it will never begin to compare in cost to the country with the greater loss through waste and inefficiency.
Let us not forget that in his report Mr. Currie put the responsibility where it belongs,
fMr. Fleming.]
at the higher levels, and if he did not carry the words "at or near the top" into the Anal edition of the report at any rate it is quite obvious from the first edition of the report that Mr. Currie had none other in mind than the responsible head of the department, and (perhaps the deputy along with him.
These facts are inescapable. But we now have additional disclosures, Mr. Speaker, since the report of the Auditor General was tabled in the house three days ago. If hon. members will take the trouble to refer to page 24 they will find that esteemed gentleman draws attention to parallel situations existing within the Department of National Defence. He points out that there are at least eight accounting systems, indicating that no sustained effort has been made to achieve uniformity in systems within the services. He catalogues a long list of problems that arise as a consequence of this diversity of accounting systems. He says there is no civilian authority answerable to parliament exercising direct control after procurement and, further on, that general efficiency is not maintained. He draws attention to some specific cases, one of which is where a brigadier received pay for a civilian position in the department for which there had been no competition, while still drawing army pay.
He also draws attention to such a case as we find in item 67, where the department authorized the purchase of a house for an area commandant for $14,000 and authorized expenditures on it of $800. Apparently these limits of authority do not mean very much in a department which is run so loosely, because we find that-
-renovation costs approximated $15,000, and these outlays were made without the consent of the deputy minister being obtained to spend in excess of $800. The result is that the house now represents an outlay of around $29,000, exclusive of materials drawn from army stores.
There, Mr. Speaker, you have proof abundant of the utter looseness of control in this department and the way in which the hard-earned money of the Canadian taxpayer is being thrown around.
Who was the brigadier?

Now, sir, I turn to the subject of the course of the debate in this house, because I have to submit to you, sir, that the house has been grossly imposed upon in the course of the debate. There have been-
Who was the brigadier?
We fired him.
Order.
These raucous interruptions sound less like human interruptions than the neighing of many horses.
Whoa!

It is not unusual at all, Mr. Speaker, for discrepancies to exist, but here we find discrepancies as between the statements of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton). The Minister of National Defence was at great pains in his speech of two days ago to stress the fact that there was no interim report. If you will look back to what was said in this house on December 4, you will recall that the minister was invited by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), at page 321, to say whether he had-
__received any positive recommendations from Mr. Currie in regard to the subject matter of his inquiry, in writing or orally, and if so is the minister prepared to convey to the house some information as to the nature of the recommendations which have been made?
The Minister of National Defence on that occasion said in reply that he had seen Mr. Currie on one occasion only. That was when he was in the department, and that he had had no other communication of whatever kind with him.
Well, Mr. Speaker, it may be that the minister had not received any formal communication from Mr. Currie, but Mr. Currie has made it abundantly clear in his report that he made a number of interim suggestions. He says:
It should be noted that interim suggestions made by me during my investigations have been already seized on, and important reforms are already being carried out.
Now, Mr. Currie obviously was making recommendations and those recommendations were being carried out in the department. They involved changes in the department. Was the Minister of National Defence so unaware of what was going on in the department that he knew nothing about these recommendations, that he knew nothing about the steps being carried out in the department to give effect to the recommendations? If that was all he knew about what was going on in the department, the minister can be deserving only of censure on the part of the house.
Hear, hear.

Then, sir, is it not only right and proper that this House of Commons should be entitled to frankness and candour on the part of the minister; that there should not have been any cavilling when there were questions asked . about interim recommendations in communications either oral or written? It is obvious that there were no written communications, but what about all these oral communications? The Leader of the Opposition was not just asking about things
Committee on Defence Expenditure Mr. Currie may have said to some officer down the line, he was asking about recommendations that had gone into the department, and the minister indicated that he knew nothing about them and took it upon himself to say that he had received no such communications.
Then, sir, let us remember this, and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) drew attention to this matter this afternoon. When the Prime Minister was asked about this matter in the house on December 17 he certainly gave the house the impression that the idea of having the draft report submitted to the department before the report was finally signed and submitted originated with Mr. Currie. You cannot read the statement of the Prime Minister in any other way. He said at page 827 of Hansard of December 17:
The inquiries also disclosed that Mr. Currie and his representatives discussed this matter with the deputy minister and that the suggestion was made that the deputy minister might go over the draft, when it was ready, and point out any inaccuracies in the facts reported which had been obtained from the department itself.
Then at page 829 he was asked if it was general practice to refer draft reports to the department in such instances. The Prime Minister expressed disapproval and said:
I have never been an investigator. I was quite surprised to learn that this investigator had felt that it was the proper thing to be done.
Yet, sir, we learn now with the tabling of the correspondence in this house two days ago that it is established beyond all question that the suggestion that that draft report should be submitted to the department emanated not from Mr. Currie but from the department. And it goes further, sir. The idea did not originate with the deputy minister; it originated with the minister himself, on his own admission in this house two days ago. He instructed the deputy minister to communicate with Mr. Currie and Mr. Currie expressed, as we can see by the correspondence, opposition to submitting the draft report, indicating that he had no intention of submitting the draft report for "vetting" in the department. Yet, apparently, pressure was continued and Mr. Currie permitted one of his officials to come up here and discuss the draft report with the deputy minister. Following that changes appear in the report, and the changes are not confined to factual matters. The changes in some cases extend to and include observations of a critical nature.
Now, sir, that leads me to make this observation, that the Prime Minister owes an apology to this house. The house was misled by the words the Prime Minister used on December 17 into thinking that this idea originated not with the deputy minister but

Committee on Defence Expenditure with Mr. Currie. The remark was made this afternoon that the Prime Minister owes an apology to Mr. Currie. I say that he does, but I also say that he owes an apology to this house and the Canadian people.
Sir, the government is trying so hard, in the face of this embarrassment, to find a scapegoat, to find a red herring, to find a way out; and that unquestionably has a good deal to do with the attempt to make capital, as they are attempting, out of the way in which knowledge came to the now absent hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and how that draft report came into his hands.
Which side are you on?
Mr. Speaker-
It was stolen.
An hon. member says it was stolen. Well, Mr. Speaker, if he has that information I suggest it is his duty to give it to the government.
Hear, hear.

Perhaps the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) will take note of the information that the hon. member indicated he possesses and will, in keeping with the tactics he is practising at the expense of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, send a letter to the hon. gentleman as he did to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, threatening him-very subtly perhaps, but threatening him nonetheless-if he does not give the information to the R.C.M.P., who have been given the distasteful and improper task of conducting this investigation, ignoring the proper law enforcement channels in this country.
Well, sir, I think the whole matter is clearly summed up in the words Sir Archibald Sinclair used in that important, and memorable debate in the British House of Commons on June 30, 1938, when dealing with the Sandys case, a directly comparable situation, he had this to say:
Governments are too apt to confuse danger to themselves with danger to the state.
Here we have a situation where a government, obsessed with its own love of power, having had power far too long for its own good is saying, in effect, that obviously this situation is not good for us. and therefore it cannot be good for the state. The Canadian people are not going to be misled by sophistry of that kind. The independence of this parliament means a great deal more to the Canadian people than to be frittered away by the methods the government is practising at the present time.
I wish to add this, sir. If complaints are made in this house about statements being

made by the chief of the general staff, they are not to be answered in the way the Prime Minister this afternoon sought to answer them. The Prime Minister ought to know, he has been in public life long enough to know, that the chief of the general staff is not precluded from voicing his opinion on matters of this kind, but there is a way to do it. The chief of the general staff or any other person, whether in the armed services or in the civilian service of the government, has a method of complaint open to him, namely to go to the minister at the head of the department. He is the man who makes the statement. The proper course of the chief of the general staff was to give his complaint to the minister, and let the minister make it. That was the proper constitutional course. Any interference with or departure from that course will be fraught with very grave dangers to the whole principle of the supremacy of the civil authority.
I add this, sir, about the way in which the government spokesmen, even the Prime Minister this afternoon, are trying to make it appear that what is involved here is an attack on the army. That is not going to impress anybody. What is involved here is not an attack on the army; it is a criticism of the Department of National Defence and the way it is being run from the top. It has been made clear times without number, it is made clear in Mr. Currie's report, that the army is not to blame. He gives credit to the army for the fact that in the face of the looseness which has prevailed throughout that Department of National Defence, the irregularities were not more grave than they were. Everyone who has spoken in this debate in this house dealing .with these exposures has been at pains to point out that the army comes out of this matter with a clean bill of health, but not the Department of National Defence and not the minister.
That is the issue, and that issue is not going to be obscured by any attempt to draw red herrings across it, because it is perfectly clear in what is being done that the government has encouraged and abetted the chief of the general staff to depart from the proper constitutional course. The chief of the general staff is quite entitled to entertain his opinions and to communicate those opinions; but the proper constitutional course is that he should communicate those opinions to the head of his department.
I am going to conclude by saying this, sir. Apparently the government is now trying to drag the matter out by proposing that the committee on defence expenditures, when it is set up, should investigate the investigator or investigate his investigation. Well, that is

quite unnecessary, sir. It would do them much more good if they were to get on with the job of cleaning up the mess which Mr. Currie has exposed.
I have nothing but the strongest words of condemnation for the adroit manoeuvre of this government in introducing an amendment to this' resolution to set up a defence expenditures committee. The very idea! The Prime Minister introduces a resolution and another minister of the government gets up and moves an amendment to it. Sir, it was a monstrous and devious device to prevent other amendments from being introduced-
Order, order.
-by members of the opposition. The responsibility for-

-preventing Mr. Currie from carrying on and completing an investigation of this department, of which after all he has investigated only one small segment, one branch of the corps of engineers, will rest with the government. If they step in and prevent Mr. Currie from being instructed to do the thing we have urged that Mr. Currie should be instructed to do, the responsibility will rest with the government and those who support them, in denying to the Canadian people the investigation of conditions in this Department of National Defence which ought to be thoroughly investigated.

There is another thing about which I am very much concerned. In our society we have four classes of people whom we trust with our secrets. One is the doctor. We allow our doctor to consult with another doctor. We have the lawyer, and when we go to him we expect him to keep our secret. Then we have the banker, and when we take our business to him we expect him to keep it secret. Finally, we have the chartered accountant; and when we consider that Mr. Currie heads that big firm of chartered accountants and he allows a leak, allows a document to get out of his possession, I say this is something that should be considered in the house, something that should be taken seriously and should not be called a red herring. We should all think about it.
The people of Canada are wondering whether their business today is going to be taken care of, whether this chartered accountant is taking care of their business, when some of those documents in his care can be taken out and given to a member of parliament.
This is a very serious situation which has now developed. So far as I am concerned it is of more concern to the people of Canada than the Currie report. It should be considered seriously. Why has this come about? Because one body of people, one splinter group in the House of Commons, think they have a right to a document that belongs to the people of Canada.
