speechtext:
Thank you. May I thank
especially the hon. member who has taken his seat.
As I said, my only purpose in intervening in the debate tonight is to deal with a point raised by the hon. member for Lake Centre this afternoon when the orders of the day were called. His question, I think, was a fair one; but I am sure that upon reflection my hon. friend will agree that it was hardly one that should be asked on orders of the day for he understands, of course, that an hon. member is not supposed to make a speech when asking such a question, nor should a speech be made when one is replying.
I take this first opportunity to deal with the question he raised. It so happens that the blue copy on which my answer is set out also contains his question. I have had a copy of his question made, and I shall now refer to it. My hon. friend asked me whether-
-any information and complaint was sworn out in connection with the incident respecting the first Currie report before the mounted police were called in to investigate.
As will be recalled my answer was that, so far as we knew, no information had been laid prior to the mounted police being asked to investigate.
Then my hon. friend asked a second question:
If there was no information under the Criminal Code, then upon what basis are the mounted police used except under the direction of the attorney general of one or other of the provinces?
And then, a little later on, taking the position that my reply to that question was not, in his view, adequate, he reframed his question as follows:
Is it possible for the Attorney General of Canada to use the R.C.M.P. for investigational work in any province without the assistance or co-operation of the attorney general of that province?
That question, I suggest, was asked in respect of an attempt which was being made
Committee on Defence Expenditure to find out what disposition had been made of a document prepared by Mr. Currie at the instance of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton). Mr. Currie himself had already at that time made a diligent effort to determine what this disposition was. He wrote in a letter from himself to the Minister of National Defence which is set out at page 977 of Hansard for January 13:
How it-
And he was referring to the document in question.
-got from the printer's shop into the hands of unauthorized third parties is still a complete mystery.
Everything which I have done by way of inquiry and investigation negatives the possibility that the copy in question could have got out in any stage or step between the printer's shop and my own organization and the department; but I still, of course, welcome any further investigation which the department or any other authority may deem it expedient to make from any angle or direction.
In the light of this suggestion, it did seem desirable to the government that it should make an investigation, and that in this connection it should use the Royal Canadian Mounted Police for that purpose. To investigate the disappearance of a document in mysterious circumstances is to carry on an investigation wholly on a voluntary basis, which really had nothing to do with the administration of justice. The federal government is in the same position in this regard as any other person interested, as a private person in, for example, the loss of property. Mr. Currie himself in this case had hired private detectives. The government utilized the services of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. There is, I suggest, no constitutional issue involved here such as I think my hon. friend's question implied, although he did not so state. The position in fact is no different from the investigation which was conducted by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the provost corps into the irregularities at Petawawa camp. The position is that where government property or some other matter of federal government concern is involved, federal authority is ample to authorize investigations such as the one in question here. I think it would seem rather a strange action for the government, confronted with the terms of Mr. Currie's letter and with the need to conduct an investigation, to go out and hire a private detective firm when it already had a very efficient police force for that purpose.
In his long and distinguished career I am sure my hon. friend must have defended a great number of cases of this kind where counsel acting against him were instructed by the federal authorities, because the fact is that the practice followed in this case is
1052	HOUSE OF
Committee on Defence Expenditure not by any means unusual. The usual practice in connection with a prosecution where the federal government has some interest, such as a breach of any statute administered by the federal government or involving fraud against or theft from the government, or even involving a criminal statute which is of national concern such as the Official Secrets Act, is that the investigation into the facts is conducted by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police or some other executive officer of the federal government, but usually the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
If the facts justify such a course, an information or complaint is laid by the federal officers just as is the case in a private prosecution. If the accused is then committed, the provincial attorney general takes over on the trial by indictment or speedy trial unless, as frequently happens where circumstances warrant it, and as they did in all of the Petawawa cases, arrangements are made by our counsel with the provincial attorney general to carry on the prosecution to completion. I know it is probably carrying coals to Newcastle, but with regard to the question of the right of the federal government- notwithstanding the fact that the administration of justice is one of the subjects assigned exclusively to the provincial government-to enforce federal statutes such as the Excise Act, the narcotics act, the Customs Act and so forth, that is fully covered in a case which I would cite for the special benefit of my hon. friend. I refer to the case of the Proprietary Articles Trade Association and others, appellants, and the Attorney General for Canada and others, respondents, reported in 1931 Appeal Cases, at page 310. I refer particularly to pages 326 and 327, and in order to clear the matter up finally I think I might read a quotation from those pages. It is not very long.

One of the arguments raised in this case, which was taken to the privy council, was that the act invaded the field of property and civil rights on the one hand or the administration of justice, each of which is a matter of provincial jurisdiction, and this is how these two arguments are

disposed of at the conclusion of the judgment. The reason I mention the property and civil rights item is that I am afraid I might be quoting a little out of context unless I did so. The portion of the judgment in question reads this way:
If then the legislation in question is authorized under one or other of the heads specifically enumerated in section 91, it is not to the purpose to say that it affects property and civil rights in the provinces. Most of the specific subjects in section 91 do affect property and civil rights but so far as the legislation of parliament in pith and substance is operating within the enumerated powers there is constitutional authority to interfere with property and civil rights. The same principle would apply to section 92, head 14, "The administration of justice in the province," even if the legislation did, as in the present case it does not, in any way interfere with the administration of justice.
The next sentence is very apt to the point I am making.
Nor is there any ground for suggesting that the dominion may not employ its own executive officers for the purpose of carrying out legislation which is within its constitutional authority, as it does regularly in the case of revenue officials and other matters which need not be enumerated.

Mr. Speaker, like most Canadians I was deeply shocked last December 15 with the main findings of the Currie report. Also, like most other Canadians, I was struck by the conclusions reached concerning government spending habits and accounting procedures noted by Canada's Auditor General in his annual report tabled this week. I have been further shocked by the apparent inclination of the government, through certain cabinet ministers and private members, to belittle these findings and also, indeed, to try to discredit the authors of these findings and to prevent a full investigation of other phases of government spending that might reveal further and perhaps far greater losses of the taxpayers' money.
Several of my colleagues have already discussed these matters in some detail. I will not deal further with the Currie report and the Sellar statements except to say that I agree completely with the policies advocated and the comments made by my colleagues. I wish, however, for the balance of my address to discuss another matter related to defence expenditure and the handling of public moneys which is of considerable concern to the house. Members of parliament are elected by the people of Canada to direct the affairs of the nation, and they have a responsibility to Canada greater than that of any other employees in the country, whether they be civil servants or members of the armed forces. A member of parliament should be, like Caesar's wife, above suspicion. We have a duty to the Canadian public, among others to scrutinize carefully the spending of the moneys levied from the taxpayer, and to the greatest possible extent eliminate waste and inefficiency, careless accounting and dishonesty in that spending. Quite properly the major share of that responsibility rests upon the members of the party forming the government. We of the opposition ranks also quite properly have a duty to the public of scrutinizing the performance of the government and pointing out to the government any action or lack of action on the part of servants of the government or members of the government which indicate failure on their part to discharge their responsibilities to the Canadian public.
In the performance of that clear duty, as a member of Her Majesty's loyal opposition I am required to bring the attention of this
Committee on Defence Expenditure house to a matter of far greater import than the amount of public money involved. It concerns, I regret to say, a member of this house. Through a presentation of the facts as I have gathered them, I trust that the member concerned, and the government of which he is a supporter, will be enabled to give to this house and the Canadian people an explanation that will clearly show this member to be in the category of Caesar's wife. And, if such an explanation cannot be given, then I trust this member and the government will take the only possible corrective action.
This matter concerns the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. George), who is also officer commanding one of the great regiments now in Canada's reserve army, the 8th Princess Louise's (New Brunswick) Hussars with headquarters at Sussex, New Brunswick. I have not had the pleasure of meeting him during my one year in the House of Commons. The Parliamentary Guide records his noteworthy career during the last world war, his service as an officer with the regiment he now commands, service in Canada, North Africa and Europe, from 1940 to 1946. He was elected to the House of Commons as a Liberal party supporter in June, 1949, representing the constituency of Westmorland.
Before going on with the facts of the matter at issue I wish to say a few words about Canada's reserve army. Like many another member of this house and many thousands of men across our nation, I have enjoyed a long and happy association with this section of our armed forces which I believe can quite properly be called Canada's vital second line of defence. As a boy bugler and signaller in the old Calgary Highlanders for some years prior to the last war, and as an N.C.O. and officer with the same reserve unit during and after the last war, I am proud of the association with so many good Canadians who have given freely of their time and efforts, without regard to monetary considerations, in order to strengthen the defences of our country.
The reserve army of today is at least as vital to Canada's defences as it was during periods of danger in the past, and this nation owes a greater debt than it generally realizes to the young and older men who, in the ranks and as officers, are giving freely of their time and efforts to maintain an effective second line of defence. The current rates of pay and allowances cannot be said to be fair and full compensation for the sacrifices of time and effort made by the great bulk of men in Canada's reserve army.
Within the ranks of the reserve army, and indeed among the great bulk of Canada's armed forces, there is a strong feeling that

Committee on Defence Expenditure all who serve should be treated fairly; that special advantages should be given to none; that those who take advantage of special situations for their own personal gain should be ruthlessly weeded out. The armed forces, I might say, are simply a cross-section of Canada's citizenry, made up of men and women of normal honesty, concerned with the welfare and security of their neighbours and their nation, as well as their own welfare and security.
In a minority of humans there is a tendency, when they see some around them taking advantage of circumstances such as inadequate or poor administration, or security of accounting, to climb aboard the gravy train and grab their share of the loot. This was true at Petawawa and certain other defence establishments in Canada about which this house already has some information. It is probably true in many other phases of Canada's $2 billion per year defence effort, where a tendency to free spending without adequate control is unfortunately becoming increasingly evident.

On a question of privilege, sir-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Before the hon. member for Fraser Valley rose on his point of order, I thought the hon. member for Calgary West was going to give some explanation of what he is doing with his notes.

Mr. Speaker, as I started to explain before being interrupted, I am dealing tonight with a subject of some delicacy and some importance to the members of this house in total, to the hon. member for Westmorland, and to myself.
Did you give him notice?

For that reason, sir, because of the delicacy of this discussion and this matter I am using extensive notes, and I hope I will have your permission to use these extensive notes of the matter on which I will now go into in more detail.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Perhaps I should intervene and inform the hon. member that it is not up to the Speaker to give permission to an hon. member to read his speech. As he knows, speeches are often read during the two long debates that take place every session, the debate on the speech from the throne and the debate on the budget. Tolerance is often exercised by the Speaker during those two long debates. When it comes to other matters before this house, especially if hon. members rise to points of order, the Speaker has no alternative but to apply the rules which are that members are supposed to express their opinions and not read speeches.
The hon. member for Fraser Valley has also mentioned the fact that the member speaking is making an attack on a member who is not present in the house. The point would be well taken if the language used by the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Nickle) were offensive or unparliamentary. There is nothing that prevents an hon. member from expressing his views, as long as he does not use unparliamentary language.
I refer the hon. member to citation 302, Beauchesne's second edition, which reads:
The Speaker feels more strongly his duty to interpose and check language which seems unparliamentary with regard to an absent member.

I noticed that the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. George) was absent. So far I have not heard any words which may be construed to be offensive or unparliamentary as applied by the hon. member for Calgary West to the member for Westmorland. The hon. member may continue.

I shall continue, not reading a speech but using my notes as a guide to what I have to say. Dealing again with the question of the hon. member for Westmorland, I may say that in recent months there has come to certain members of this house, including myself, information to the effect that unduly large pay and allowances have been claimed by and paid to this member in his reserve army capacity. That information, from sources I will not name, was sufficient to justify further investigation.
During the last session of this house a series of questions was placed on the order paper by my colleague, the hon. member for Wentworth (Mr. Lennard). The questions were designed to obtain complete information as to pay and allowances of reserve force officers in Canada's four army commands during the calendar year 1951, in all cases where the year's payments exceeded $800. The answers were tabled in this house on Friday, November 21 last, following the opening of the current session. The answers listed by name and rank 260 officers of the reserve force, ranging from brigadiers down to captains, who received in pay and allowances for their services to Canada in the year 1951 amounts exceeding $800. The average amount received was under $1,000.
There was only one payment on that long list exceeding $2,000. This was the amount of $2,495.01 that was paid to Lieutenant Colonel E. W. George, who is the hon. member for Westmorland. The amount of pay and allowances to him was about double the average payment to all other lieutenant colonels on the list, and was about $770 more than the second highest payment to an officer of the same rank. At the rate of pay in effect during 1951, $367 per month for lieutenant colonels, the hon. member received army pay for a total of 204 full days in that year, if it were assumed that the total sum paid did not include some expense allowance.
It may be assumed, of course, that some expense allowance was included, and the number of days of actual army pay would represent less than 204 days.
It is of interest, however, to note that the second highest payment to reserve force officers was to a brigadier, who received $1,884.87 in pay and allowances or $610 less than the hon. member. At the prevailing brigadier's rate of pay, $689 per month, and assuming
Committee on Defence Expenditure that the total payment did not include any expense allowance, the highest paid reserve brigadier claimed pay for service totalling only 82 days. Now, it might be logically assumed that Colonel George claimed army pay for a greater number of days of service than any other reserve officer because he actually devoted many more days and part days to the command of his reserve army regiment than any other reserve army officer in the country. As most, hon. members are doubtless aware, attendance at two parades of a reserve unit entitles a man or officer to one day's pay. In addition, full pay is allowed for service days in annual training camp, and for days devoted to administrative duties. Presumably, Colonel George devoted a sufficient number of part and full days to his duties as officer commanding his regiment to qualify for the pay and allowances claimed and paid. The only question that could be raised was as to why his number of service days should have been so much greater than that of other officers of similar rank and responsibility in the reserve forces.
This week a further question was raised with the tabling of the public accounts of Canada for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1952. A check of the latest public accounts, covering nine months of 1951, the year for which Colonel George's army payments are on record, coupled with a study of the public accounts for the previous year, which included the other three months, makes my statement of today necessary.
During the calendar year 1951 the House of Commons sat for 142 days during the session period January 29 to June 30, and for a further 82 days between October 9 and December 29 of that year. These periods total some 224 days out of 1951.
The public accounts show that the hon. member for Westmorland claimed sessional indemnities and expense allowances in their maximum amounts for attendance in the House of Commons during the calendar year 1951. Allowing the full 15 days of absence, on grounds other than illness, permitted before deduction from indemnities, the hon. member presumably attended in parliament some 209 days in 1951. It therefore appears obvious, sir, that in his dual capacity as a member of this house and as officer commanding a reserve army regiment, the member for Westmorland claimed for and received from public funds payment for more days in 1951 than there are days in a calendar year. It must be assumed that he devoted no time whatsoever in 1951 to his personal affairs or running his farm in New Brunswick.

Committee on Defence Expenditure
The hon. member, sir, and this government of which he is a member, should without delay make a full explanation to this house, and to the public of Canada, as to the rather extraordinary situation disclosed in the answers given my colleague, the hon. member for Wentworth, by the Department of National Defence, coupled with the information contained in the public accounts of Canada. Inasmuch as no public returns are yet available for the calendar year 1952, I would suggest that the answers to be given might also include full information as to the year just concluded.
The situation, sir, is one requiring full explanation because of the unique position of responsibility to Canada occupied by all members of this parliament. It requires full explanation, too, because of the special responsibility placed in all commissioned officers of Canada's armed forces. Full explanation is particularly necessary in this case, sir, because the hon. member for Westmorland is one of the government party members of the committee on defence expenditure, charged with the specific task of analysing and checking the vast expenditures for defence being made by our nation.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Before I recognize any other speaker-it is now ten o'clock in any event-I should like to say a word in connection with the remarks that have been made by the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Nickle). I am only making these remarks at this stage as a caveat because I am not quite sure of the exact status of the accusations which have been made in the course of this debate by the hon. member against the member for Westmorland (Mr. George).

I just want to leave this thought with hon. members. It might well be that this type of accusation-which after all could mean that a breach of privilege has been committed by the hon. member for Westmorland-would be of the type that should be referred to the standing committee on privileges and elections. If that is so, I think it should be done by a distinct motion. As I say, I am not sure of the point. I was merely looking it up. It may be that the matter will be pursued by other hon. members in the course of this debate. This is a motion to set up a committee to examine the expenditures made by the defence department. There is no question that the expenditure referred to has been made and that it appears in the public accounts. But as to the point that this money referred to as paid by the Department of National Defence has been received by a member of this house, that matter may well constitute, as in the opinion of the hon. member it seems to, a breach of privilege and might, I submit, well be of the type that has to be referred to the standing committee on privileges and elections. It therefore might be out of order to discuss it on this motion. I am not making a ruling. I just want to give this point further thought and to consult Mr. Speaker about it. However, I wanted these remarks to be made before the matter is concluded.
On motion of Mr. Cruickshank the debate was adjourned.
